messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I glance up the lane where Hesper was looking, watching for anyone lingering or taking an interest in her door. Then I step inside first, sword sheathed, shield held low, and make room for the others.

“Best talk out of the street.” I keep my voice quiet. “Who are you watching for, Mistress Vallow—and what do you need done before nightfall?”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa steps in past the threshold, the little beads at her wrist clicking once as she moves. She doesn't rush; she keeps her hands visible and her voice low.

"You've got the shutters shut on a fine morning, Mistress Vallow. Something out there you don't like the look of, or something in here you want kept from the sun?"

The words are quiet, not needling. She glances around the dim hall as her eyes adjust, looking less at the woman than at the shape of the house — exits, stairs, whether anyone else is breathing in the shadows.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell catches where her eyes go and lets his own follow — a slow, idle turn of the head up the lane toward the main street, as if he's only taking in the morning. Who's standing about, who isn't working, which shutters across the way are open and which aren't.

Then he steps off the step and through the door, first, because someone has to and he'd rather be inside a dim hall than framed in a doorway.

"Shutters closed and a glance up the street like that," he says quietly as he passes her, not unkindly. "Whoever you're expecting, I'd like to know their face before I'm out there after dark looking for it. Inside's fine for the telling."

scenes.narration:
Bram turns his head up the lane, the way he'd look over a stretch of road with too many trees beside it. A step behind him, Pell does the same, slowly and idly, a man taking in the morning.

Bram picks out two people at the top of the lane, where it meets the main street.

The first is easy to see. A tiefling in a road-dusty coat leans on the wall of the cooper's yard at the corner, tail wrapped close around one boot, looking at the cobbles as if he has lost something there. He has been standing a while; the dust on his shoulders hasn't been brushed off. Every so often he looks at the cooper's gate, then away again.

The second is harder, and Bram nearly misses him. A boy of fourteen or so sits on the rim of the horse trough on the main-street side, bare-armed, a stable lad by his clothes, the kind Beregost has fifty of. He's doing nothing much. But when Hesper's door swung open his head came round to it, and it took him a heartbeat too long to look away. Since then he hasn't once looked down the lane, and nobody manages that by accident.

Pell sees the tiefling too: the dusty coat, the loitering, the glances. The rest of the street looks like a street to him. Carters, a woman with a basket, smoke from the forges. Nothing else catches his eye on the way in.

Inside, the door thuds shut behind the three of you and the hall goes brown and dim, lit only by the strips of sun round the shutters. Sefa's eyes adjust. A narrow stair rises on the right. A door on the left stands open on a front room with a writing desk and a cold hearth, and a passage at the back runs to a kitchen and what must be the yard door. The house smells of ink, cold ashes and beeswax. Apart from your own breathing she hears only Hesper's, and a clock ticking somewhere upstairs. If anyone else is in the house, they're keeping very still.

Hesper slides the bolt across. She stays with her back to the door a moment, and then she answers the questions in order, one at a time, like a woman going down a list.

"A boy has stood at the top of my lane for three days. He doesn't work there and he isn't anyone's. I don't know who sends him." She looks at Sefa. "The shutters are for him. There is nothing in here that needs keeping from the sun."

She goes into the front room, takes a folded paper off the desk and holds it out to whoever is nearest. It's a moneylender's notice in a clerk's tidy hand: *Gaspar Thole, at the sign of the Scales, Beregost. Item pledged by Master Aubrey Vallow, notary: one iron coffer, sealed. Term expires at sundown this day. The right to the forfeit has been purchased by Master Corwen Ashby.*

"My husband was Aubrey Vallow. He sealed contracts in this town for twenty years. He died last winter. He fell on the steps of the Song of the Morning." She says it flatly, as if she has said it often enough to wear the words smooth. "Eight months ago he pledged that coffer to Thole, and I didn't know until that notice came. His papers hold no pledge ticket. Without one, Thole says, the thing isn't mine to redeem, widow or not."

She folds her ink-stained hands.

"So these are the terms. You bring me that coffer before sundown. You bring it to me unopened, with the seal whole. That is the one condition, and it isn't open to discussion. How you get it out of Thole is your business. I would prefer you did it within the law of this town, but I'm not hiring you for your manners. Fifty gold now, a hundred on delivery. If it goes to this Ashby instead, you keep the fifty and we're quits."

Then she waits, looking from Bram to Sefa to Pell. She doesn't say what is in the coffer, and she doesn't say why the boy at the trough worries her.

 Pell's look up the lane gets him only half of it. He takes in the tiefling at the cooper's wall and files him as the one worth watching. His eyes pass straight over the boy on the rim of the horse trough, and Pell leaves the street believing there's one watcher out there, not two.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“The boy’s at the horse trough now. Watched your door open, then made a business of not watching it. There’s a dusty-coated tiefling by the cooper’s yard too, though his interest seemed to be in their gate.”

I look over the notice, then back to Hesper.

“I’ll leave your seal alone. But I’m not agreeing to rob a moneylender before we’ve tried speaking to him. How much is owed, and is redemption money separate from our pay?”

I tap Ashby’s name on the paper. “Who is he to you or your husband? If we’re walking into a quarrel, we need to know whose.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa leans to read the notice as it passes, then looks back to Hesper, her voice calm and low.

"This isn't an errand, Mistress Vallow. It's a dispute with a moneylender and a buyer who's already paid for the forfeit. So before I touch your coin: whose seal is on that coffer — your husband's, or Thole's? And did Aubrey keep any copy of the pledge anywhere at all? A line in a ledger, a note to a clerk, a receipt from the Scales. Even a memory of the day he carried it there would help. Then tell me about Ashby. Is he the kind of man who sends a boy to watch a widow's door?"

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell takes the notice, tilts it toward a strip of shutter-light and reads it twice, the way he was taught to read anything with a sum attached — once for what it says and once for what it leaves out.

"Tiefling, your boy. Road dust on him three days old, watching the cooper's gate as much as your door. He's waiting on someone as well as watching you." He hands the paper on to Bram. "That's what I saw, for what it's worth."

He leans a shoulder on the desk, easy, not touching anything else.

"Now the questions a man asks before he says yes. Thole — does he keep the coffer at the Scales, or does he bank it somewhere with thicker walls? Does he know you by sight? And Ashby. Who is he to your husband that he'd buy a forfeit eight months in the making the very week it falls due? A man doesn't pay for the right to a locked box unless he knows what's in it."

A short pause.

"And the seal. I'll say this plainly so there's no misunderstanding later: I open locks for a living, and I'm telling you I won't open yours. Unopened, seal whole, into your hands. But if Thole's already broken it — or Ashby has — I want to know now what you'd have us do, because I'd rather not learn your answer at sundown with the thing in my arms."

scenes.narration:
Hesper hears all three of them out without interrupting. Then she takes the questions in the order they were asked, as if ticking down a column.

"The boy at the trough. Yes, that's him. Fourteen or so, bare arms." She glances at Pell. "Not the tiefling, Master Dunmore. I've watched the boy for three days. I only noticed the tiefling yesterday afternoon, and he's never once looked at my windows. I don't know what he's waiting for."

She turns back to Bram.

"How much is owed, I can't tell you. I asked Thole twice. He says the sum is a matter between him and the bearer of the ticket, and I have no ticket. If he'll take money, find out his figure and bring it to me before you pay anything. I won't have a sum paid in my name that I haven't seen. And yes, the redemption is separate. Fifty now and a hundred on delivery is for your work. Anything owed to Thole is my debt to settle."

She lays one finger beside Ashby's name on the notice.

"I don't know him. He's nothing to me, and his name isn't anywhere in Aubrey's papers. People at market say he came to town this spring and buys iron for some firm. That's everything I know. I haven't said he sends the boy, and I won't say it until I know."

She turns to Sefa.

"The seal isn't Thole's, and it isn't Aubrey's notary mark. I know his mark. I sealed his letters with it for twenty years. The wax on the coffer is pale, nearly gold, and there's a sun pressed into it. I never saw him set it, and I don't know whose it is." Her mouth thins. "As for copies, there are none. I've been through his papers twice: his daybook, his letter-book, his drawers. There's no ticket, no receipt, not one line about the Scales. The coffer sat in his study for years. He told me to keep it shut, and I did. One morning last winter he went out with it under his arm and came back without it. He said it was safe. I didn't ask him where. A month later he was dead."

She says that part flatly too, and goes straight on to Pell.

"Thole keeps it at the Scales, in a strongroom behind the counting-room. He showed it to me through a grate, on a shelf. He wanted me to see it was whole, and it was, three days ago. He knows my face. I've been in his shop twice this week, and he was civil both times and gave me nothing." A short pause. "Why a man would buy that forfeit in the very week it falls due, I've asked myself the same question. I don't have an answer for you."

"Your last question is a fair one, so here's the clause. If the seal is broken before the coffer comes into your hands, you bring it to me anyway, and you tell me who broke it. If you can show me it wasn't you, the hundred is still yours. If it breaks in your hands, it isn't."

She takes a small leather purse from the desk drawer and sets it on the blotter. She keeps her hand on it and doesn't push it across.

"Those are the terms. Do you take them?"

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“I’ll take the work on those terms.” I glance at Sefa and Pell, leaving them their own answer.

“Give us a short signed note authorising us to speak to Thole for you. He may still refuse, but let’s give him one less excuse. And may we carry the notice?”

I settle my shield strap. “I’d start at the Scales. Ask what proof he’ll accept without the ticket, find his price, and see whether the seal’s still whole. No promises of payment until you’ve approved the sum.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa doesn't move toward the purse. She stands with her arms folded loosely, so the beads don't click, and looks at Hesper with a healer's patience.

"I'll take it. But before my hand touches any money, one thing you should know about how I work."

She lets the dim settle a moment.

"There's a boy outside who's been put where he is by someone with no better use for a child than to spend him watching a widow's house. If this goes badly, he's the first one hurt — run off, picked up by the Watch, or marked as a failed watcher. I'd prefer to speak to him before anyone frightens him. A copper and a kind word can do what a cudgel can't. I won't have him swept aside as part of the scenery." Her voice is still level. "If he's Ashby's, or someone's worse, he may tell us more in two minutes than an hour at Thole's counter."

She uncrosses her arms.

"You've said you want the coffer unopened and the seal whole. I'll add my own condition: I want to see it with my own eyes, the way you did, before we pay or promise anything. Through a grate or otherwise. I can read what's there — the wax, the fittings, the dust on the shelf. And I can tell you if it's been moved since you saw it."

Then, more gently:

"Aubrey kept it shut for years, took it out in winter, and came home without it saying it was safe. A month later he fell on temple steps. You may not want to know the rest, and I won't press you to open that door. But if there's anything about the box that would make men kill for it — a debt, a secret, a thing that shouldn't exist — tell us only yes or no, and to whom you've already spoken. We can do the rest without a name."

She glances at the purse, unreadable. "Fifty now, a hundred at the door at sundown, unopened. I understand the terms. I'd like your answer."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell looks at the purse a moment, then at her hand on it, and doesn't reach for it yet.

"Gold wax, a sun pressed in it. Your husband died on Lathander's steps." He says it quietly, not as an accusation. "I'd wager the Song of the Morning knows that seal, even if you don't. Worth an hour of someone's day to ask them, before we go kicking on Thole's door."

He straightens off the desk.

"I take the terms. Fifty now, a hundred on delivery, seal whole or the name of who broke it." A glance to Bram and Sefa. "I'd do it in this order, if nobody objects: the Scales first, in daylight, with the door open and honest faces in front. Bram asks Thole his figure, since Thole will take a figure from a man with a shield sooner than from me. While he's naming it, I'd like a look at that grate and the shelf behind it — how the strongroom's built, what the lock is, where the back of the building gives onto. Not to use. To know. If Thole's reasonable, Mistress Vallow pays and that's the end of it. If he isn't, or if Ashby's already been in the room, then we know what we're dealing with before dark instead of after."

He takes the purse now, weighs it once in his palm, and tucks it inside his coat.

"One more thing. Your boy at the trough — I'd rather he didn't follow us to the Scales. I'll go out your yard door and come round. Let him count two leaving, not three."

scenes.narration:
Hesper hears the three of them out. When Pell reaches for the purse she lifts her hand from it and lets him take it.

"Fifty," she says. "Count it if you like."

Then she sits down at the desk, pulls a clean sheet toward her and dips the pen. She takes the questions in the order she was given them.

"Master Halloway. Yes, you'll have your note." The pen scratches steadily in a plain clerk's hand, with no flourish on any letter. She doesn't read it back. She turns it round on the blotter so he can read it himself:

*To Master Gaspar Thole, at the sign of the Scales. The bearers, Bram Halloway, Sefa Marrin and Pell Dunmore, speak for me in the matter of the iron coffer pledged by my late husband, Aubrey Vallow. They may hear your terms. They may not agree to any sum on my behalf. — Hesper Vallow, widow.*

She signs it and blots it. Her eyes go to the small brass seal-press at the corner of the desk, and she leaves it where it is. "I won't put his mark on it. It isn't mine to use." She folds the note in three and hands it to Bram, with Thole's notice on top. "Carry both. Bring the notice back to me. It's the only paper I have from that man."

She turns to Sefa.

"The boy. He's a child, and I have no quarrel with him. Speak to him if you think it's worth it. Don't do it on my step." That part comes out a little sharper than the rest. "As for seeing the coffer, the grate is Thole's to open, not mine. I've no objection. Whether he'll show it to strangers, I can't say."

She stops. When she answers the last part, she says it as flatly as she said the part about the temple steps.

"You asked yes or no. I can't honestly give you either. He told me to keep it shut, and he never told me why. I've spoken of that coffer to Gaspar Thole, twice, this week. Not to the Fist. Not to the temple. Not to any friend. Now I've spoken of it to you three, and that's everyone."

Last, she turns to Pell.

"The temple. I haven't taken the seal to them. Ask, if you think it's worth an hour. Leave my name out of it if you can." She doesn't explain that. "The yard door is at the end of the passage. It's barred on the inside. It gives onto the yard, and the yard gate onto the back alley that runs behind the lane. You come out near the forges, below the main street, out of sight of the trough."

She caps the inkpot. A strip of light from round the shutter has crept a finger's width across the floor while she wrote.

"The sum comes to me before anything is paid. You know the rest." She folds her ink-stained hands on the blotter. "I'll be here until sundown."

The hall waits for you, with the front door bolted and the yard door barred at the end of the passage. Nothing else happens in the house unless one of you wants it to.

"You've said you want the coffer unopened and the seal whole. I'll add my own condition: I want to see it with my own eyes, the way you did, before we pay or promise anything. Through a grate or otherwise. I can read what's there — the wax, the fittings, the dust on the shelf. And I can tell you if it's been moved since you saw it."

Then, more gently:

"Aubrey kept it shut for years, took it out in winter, and came home without it saying it was safe. A month later he fell on temple steps. You may not want to know the rest, and I won't press you to open that door. But if there's anything about the box that would make men kill for it — a debt, a secret, a thing that shouldn't exist — tell us only yes or no, and to whom you've already spoken. We can do the rest without a name."

She glances at the purse. You can't read her face. "Fifty now, a hundred at the door at sundown, unopened. I understand the terms. I'd like your answer."

When you reach for the purse, Hesper lifts her hand from it and lets you take it.

"Fifty," she says. "Count it if you like."

Hesper has heard the three of you out. She sits down at the desk, pulls a clean sheet toward her and dips the pen. She answers the questions in the order they were put to her.

"Master Halloway. Yes, you'll have your note." The pen scratches steadily in a plain clerk's hand, with no flourish on any letter. She doesn't read it back. She turns it round on the blotter so Bram can read it himself:

*To Master Gaspar Thole, at the sign of the Scales. The bearers, Bram Halloway, Sefa Marrin and Pell Dunmore, speak for me in the matter of the iron coffer pledged by my late husband, Aubrey Vallow. They may hear your terms. They may not agree to any sum on my behalf. — Hesper Vallow, widow.*

She signs it and blots it. Her eyes go to the small brass seal-press at the corner of the desk, and she leaves it where it is. "I won't put his mark on it. It isn't mine to use." She folds the note in three and hands it to Bram, with Thole's notice on top. "Carry both. Bring the notice back to me. It's the only paper I have from that man."

She turns to Sefa.

"The boy. He's a child, and I have no quarrel with him. Speak to him if you think it's worth it. Don't do it on my step." That part comes out a little sharper than the rest. "As for seeing the coffer, the grate is Thole's to open, not mine. I've no objection. Whether he'll show it to strangers, I can't say."

She stops. When she answers the last part, she says it as flatly as she spoke of the temple steps.

"You asked yes or no. I can't honestly give you either. He told me to keep it shut, and he never told me why. I've spoken of that coffer to Gaspar Thole, twice, this week. Not to the Fist. Not to the temple. Not to any friend. Now I've spoken of it to you three, and that's everyone."

Last, she turns to you.

"The temple. I haven't taken the seal to them. Ask, if you think it's worth an hour. Leave my name out of it if you can." She doesn't explain that. "The yard door is at the end of the passage. It's barred on the inside. It gives onto the yard, and the yard gate onto the back alley that runs behind the lane. You come out near the forges, below the main street, out of sight of the trough."

She caps the inkpot. A strip of light from round the shutter has crept a finger's width across the floor while she wrote.

"The sum comes to me before anything is paid. You know the rest." She folds her ink-stained hands on the blotter. "I'll be here until sundown."

The hall waits for you, with the front door bolted and the yard door barred at the end of the passage. Nothing else happens in the house unless one of you wants it to.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I read the note, then tuck both papers safely away.

“You’ll have your notice back.”

In the hall, I speak quietly to the others. “Sefa, if you want a word with the lad, I’ll leave the talking to you. I’ll stay a few paces off—close enough to help, not looming over him. Pell, we’ll meet you at the Scales unless you’ve something else in mind.”

Once Sefa is ready, I unbolt the front door and step out, leaving my sword sheathed. I look toward the trough to see whether the boy is still there, then make room for her to lead.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa gives Hesper a small nod, not a bow. "We'll bring you word before any coin changes hands. If a stranger comes asking about us before sundown, tell him you've hired a guard, not three names."

She turns to Pell. "Go on, then. Give us a count of thirty before you slip out the back. If you can, hold at the lane's end where you can still see the boy and the street both. I want to know if he has a friend who moves when we do."

Then to Bram, quietly: "Walk with me and hang your shield easy. Let me speak to the boy first. Two of us closing in on a fourteen-year-old by a trough will turn him into a runner, and runners tell no one anything."

She moves toward the front hall and waits by the door for the bolt, hands loose at her sides.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell nods once, like a man who's heard a contract read out and found nothing in it to argue with.

"Then I'll see you at sundown, Mistress Vallow. Earlier, if Thole's a reasonable man." A beat. "He won't be. They never are the week the term falls due."

He turns to Bram and Sefa in the dim.

"Go out the front, the pair of you, slow and plain, the way you came. Let the boy have his count. Sefa, if you want your two minutes with him, take them on the walk — away from this step, as the lady asks. I'll be at the Scales before you are. Don't look for me; I'll find you. If I'm not at Thole's counter when you get there, I'm looking at the back of his building, and I'll come in the front door like a customer when I'm done."

To Hesper, already moving toward the passage: "The Scales — which street, and what's it stand between? I'd rather not ask a cooper for directions with a tiefling leaning on his wall."

He goes down the passage to the kitchen, lifts the bar on the yard door quietly, and eases it open a crack first — looking the yard over, then the gate, then the alley beyond it, for anyone who's thought of the back way before he did. Only then does he slip out, draws the door to behind him, and goes for the alley and the forges below the main street, keeping to the side the smoke drifts along.

scenes.narration:
Hesper answers Sefa first.

"I'll tell anyone who asks that I've hired help. Your names are nobody's business, and they won't get them from me." Then, to Pell, as he's already turning for the passage: "Main street, toward the temple. Four doors past the Red Sheaf, on the same side, between a chandler's and a saddler's. A brass scale hangs over the door." She doesn't answer what he said about Thole being unreasonable.

Pell doesn't wait for the bolt. He's gone down the passage before Bram reaches the front door.

---

**At the back.** The kitchen is cold and tidy, with one cup upturned on the drainboard. Pell lifts the bar off its brackets without a scrape and opens the yard door a crack. He sees a woodpile under a lean-to, an empty washing line and a water butt. The gate in the far wall is shut and latched. He crosses to it, lifts the latch, and looks through the gap along the alley beyond.

It's a back alley like a hundred in the Lower City, only cleaner. It runs between the backs of the lane houses and somebody's kitchen gardens, then slopes down toward the forges, and the coal smoke lies along it at head height. A cat sits on a wall. Nobody stands in a doorway, nobody looks out of a window, and nobody is waiting. The back way is empty.

He draws the gate shut behind him and goes down the alley on the smoky side. Below, the alley opens onto a yard behind two smithies. Apprentices in leather aprons are hauling a cart of bar iron. They glance at him and away again, the way busy people look at a man walking past. A gap between a forge and a stable leads him onto the lanes behind the main street, and he follows them toward the temple bell-tower over the roofs. The Red Sheaf is easy to pick out from behind by its stable yard and the smell of horses. He counts four buildings past it.

The back of the Scales is not a shop front. It's a narrow house of dressed grey stone, three storeys high. On the ground floor a wall closes in a yard, with an oak gate strapped in iron. The gate has no keyhole on the outside, so it's barred from within. Above the wall he sees a barred window with its shutters latched, and a kitchen chimney with a thin thread of smoke. The back corner is different. That stretch of stone is newer and paler, set without any window at all, with one narrow air-slit high up, crossed by an iron grille. On the second floor a shutter stands open. A woman in a cap leans out and shakes a cloth, then pulls her head back in.

Something moves behind the yard gate as Pell's shadow crosses it. A heavy chain drags over the cobbles, and he hears breathing low and deep, from something much bigger than a lapdog. It doesn't bark. It just knows he is there.

---

**At the front.** Bram slides the bolt and opens the door onto full morning. After the dim hall the lane is very bright. Hammers ring and the smoke comes up from the forges. He looks up the lane first.

The boy is still on the trough rim, bare arms and all. So is the tiefling, his back to the cooper's wall and his tail wound round his boot.

Sefa steps out first and Bram follows, a couple of paces behind and off to the side. The shield hangs low on his arm. Behind them the door shuts, and they hear the bolt go home.

They're halfway up the lane when the tiefling notices them. A woman, and a big man in chain coming straight up the lane toward his corner. He straightens off the wall and takes half a step toward the cooper's gate, as if he means to knock at last. Then he stops and stays where he is, looking anywhere but at Bram. He has the stiff face of a man who has been moved on from corners before.

The boy took in the door opening, and he took in the count: two came out. Now he slides off the trough rim, cups water in both hands and splashes it over his forearms. He scrubs at them as if nothing in Beregost matters more than this. He keeps his head down. His feet are under him, though, and his weight is on the side toward the main street.

Sefa reaches the top of the lane. The trough is a few steps away, and the boy is close enough to hear her without anyone raising their voice. He hasn't run yet.

messages.text:
I stop a few paces short of the trough, leaving the boy’s way onto the main street clear. I turn slightly aside, shield low, and let Sefa speak without adding a word.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa stops a stride short of the trough and raises one hand a little, not to him — a small "hold" for Bram behind her. She leaves the path to the main street open on the boy's side.

"Morning's warming up," she says lightly, nodding at the water. "You look like you've been at that trough three days running. They'll start charging you for it, if it's a service." She doesn't put her hands on her hips or block him. Her voice is easy, pitched under the hammer-ring from the forges, so he has to listen without being called out in the street.

"I'm Sefa." She says it like an introduction, not a demand. "I was a healer down the Gate, but I sat plenty of mornings like this outside the hospice, waiting on somebody else's business to finish. Long work, standing about. Hot too." She gestures with her chin at his wet forearms. "That's not a bad trick."

She turns a little, so her shoulder is toward him, not her chest, and glances once down the lane they came from, then back, making herself mild.

"I'm not Watch, and I'm not the Fist. I won't put rough hands on you, and I won't ask you to give up anyone's name where it can come back on you. But I'd like five minutes of your time, away from your corner friend there." She doesn't look at the tiefling. "I've a copper in it for you, just to talk. You can walk off any time you like."

She waits a beat, one foot ready to step back if he bolts.

"Fair?"

cards.title: Persuasion: getting the boy at the trough to stay and talk instead of running

presses.text:
The boy's hands slow in the water and stop. He doesn't run. He doesn't stand, either. He pulls his forearms out of the trough, wipes them on his shirt, and looks up at you again, and this time he meets your eyes for longer than a glance.

"Fair," he says, so quietly you barely catch it under the hammers. His voice hasn't finished breaking. When he stands, he keeps his own path to the main street open and nearly open both. He is a thin, plain-faced boy with red knuckles and one shirt that doesn't fit his shoulders.

"I know why you've come," he says. "You've been in at the widow's." It isn't a question. "You're going to the moneylender's. She's hired the three of you to carry it for her." The third of you — Pell — is already away by the back.

He doesn't break his neck to look around. His eyes go to the tiefling and off again, like a man noting weather.

"Your copper, I'll have it for that," he says, "since I've told you, and no more." He means the fact that she had three of you, or that he's been set here. "I watch the house. Not her, not the lane, not the comings — the house. Who goes in, who comes out, who has it watched besides me. That's my work. I don't go near her door, and I never have." His feet shift under him, not to run yet. "If you're finished, I'd sooner you moved on."

He stands there, wet sleeves and all, waiting to see what you do with it.
presses.reply:
Thanks, that's a vivid picture of the boy, and I can see the scene you're hoping for. I can't take it as what happens, though. What he says, what he knows and whether he stays are mine to play, and the die on your card decides how he takes Sefa's approach. The card is still waiting, and I'm keeping it: a nervous lad with his weight already on the main-street side might well bolt from a stranger, so the outcome is genuinely uncertain.

What I need from you is Sefa's side of the moment. What does she say to him as she reaches the trough, and how does she stand? Does the copper come out at once, or only after he's spoken? Write that as Sefa, then press the roll. I'll play the boy from that and from the result, in the next turn.

One thing I'll say now so it doesn't surprise you later: anything he knows comes from what he could actually have seen or been told. He doesn't simply know what happened inside the house or by the back way. Whatever he reveals, I'll make sure it has a source.

presses.text:
Sefa doesn't bring out the copper yet. She lets her raised hand fall and takes one half-step nearer the trough, not into his path.

"It's written all over that shield they're going to the moneylender's." She keeps her voice light, but not mocking. "Men like that go straight to the counting room. It'll be all right." Her eyes flick to the main street once, then back.

"The copper's yours when I've asked what I came to ask. You can walk off before then, and I won't stop you." She pauses. "You just told me you watch the house, not her. So you've likely got better eyes than most, and a steadier arse on that rim than half the Watch. I'd rather buy a cup of water for a boy who's good at standing about than for one who runs his mouth."

She doesn't crouch. She stays her own height, but lets her shoulder fall soft.

"Who goes in and out, you said. Before I was in there, three of us went up the lane and through the oak." She studies him a moment. "Were we the first to go in today?"
presses.reply:
Thanks, I'll play Sefa's approach just as you wrote it: no copper yet, a half-step closer without blocking his path, standing at her own height, and the offer that he can walk off before she's done.

One thing to fix before the die. The boy hasn't said a word in play yet. Two of Sefa's lines, "You just told me you watch the house, not her" and "Who goes in and out, you said," lean on lines from your earlier proposal, and those never happened. So I'll play them as Sefa guessing out loud about him, and he'll hear a stranger guessing what he does. If you'd rather she put it another way, say so now. Otherwise that's how it goes.

She also says out loud, on the street, that the other two are going to the moneylender's. That's Sefa's call. I'll play it as said, in the open, a few steps from the cooper's wall.

The Persuasion card stays as it is, DC 15. He's a nervous lad with his weight already on the main-street side, and that's what the die is for. Roll it, and I'll play the boy from your words and the result.

scenes.narration:
Sefa stops a stride short of the trough with one hand raised a little behind her. Bram stops where she wants him. The boy keeps scrubbing his forearms, slower now, and listens without looking up. His eyes come up at "I'm not Watch." He looks at her, then over her shoulder at Bram's shield, then back at her hands.

The boy takes his weight off the street-side foot. Not much, but he does it.

"He's not my friend." He jerks his chin at the tiefling without turning his head. "Don't know him. He's been stood there since yesterday looking at Dobb's gate like it owes him money." He wipes his wet hands down his shirt and looks Sefa over again, the beads, the plain knife, the face that isn't angry. "I'm Wat."

He glances once along the main street toward the Red Sheaf, then back.

"A copper's a copper," he says, and his ears go a little red. "But I get a silver for sitting here. I'm not giving that up for one copper and a talk." He keeps his voice under the hammers, the way she did. "And I'm not walking off anywhere with him." He means Bram. "You want to talk, we talk here, by the trough, where people can see. And you don't tell anyone I did. Nobody. Swear it?"

He stays put, rubbing the water off his arms. He's waiting for her answer, and his feet are still ready to run.

Bram keeps his eyes past the boy, on the main street. A carter backs a dray of staves toward the cooper's gate. Two apprentices go by with a bar of iron between them on a pole. An old man sweeps the step of the Red Sheaf down the street. Nobody stops, nobody turns to watch the woman at the trough, and nobody walks off quickly. As far as Bram can see, nobody in the street is watching except the boy. At the wall the tiefling lets his shoulders down once they've walked past him, and he goes back to looking at the cooper's gate.

 Sefa's easy voice and open hands do their work. Wat decides she isn't trouble, and he stays at the trough to hear her out instead of bolting for the main street.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell doesn't break stride. A man who stops at a gate with a dog behind it is a man the dog remembers; a man who walks past is just the morning. He lets his shadow slide off the planks and keeps going, hands in sight, eyes doing the work.

*Newer stone, no window, an air-slit a cat couldn't fit through. That's the strongroom, and Thole built it after he'd learned something.* He marks it against the house — back corner, ground floor, under the second-storey shutter the woman in the cap leans out of — and marks the chained thing in the yard with it. Not a lock problem. A dog problem, which is worse, because dogs don't have a tolerance for patience.

He glances up once, idle, at the roofline: how the Scales meets the saddler's and the chandler's either side, whether the eaves run together or there's a gap, where a man on the roof would be seen from. Then he's round the end of the row, between the saddler's and whatever stands next to it, and out onto the main street a few doors down from the brass scale, brushing forge-smoke from his coat like a man who's come from the smithies with nothing on his mind but money.

He finds a spot across the way where he can see Thole's door and the street toward the Red Sheaf both — a wall to lean on, or a stall to pretend interest in — and waits for Bram and Sefa to come up from the lane, counting who else is on the street and whether anyone walks when they walk.

scenes.narration:
Pell lets his shadow slide off the gate planks and keeps walking. Behind the wall the chain drags once more over the cobbles, then goes still. The dog doesn't bark, and it doesn't follow him along the wall. It heard a man go by, and that is all it heard.

He looks up once at the roofs as he goes, the way he'd look at weather. Reading a roofline is his trade, and this one is easy to read. The Scales stands a full storey taller than both its neighbours. On the chandler's side the chandler's roof runs right up against Thole's wall. It's old slate, mossy at the ridge, with a chimney stack a man could crouch behind. Above it Thole's third floor rises bare, with one small shuttered window and nothing to hold on to but the joints in the dressed stone. On the saddler's side there's a gap between the houses, a ginnel no wider than a man's shoulders and choked with broken crates. The saddler's eaves stop short of Thole's wall by about three feet. Anyone up there would be in plain view of the back windows of the lane houses, and of anyone hanging out washing in the gardens. On the near side the Scales has no back door at all, only the yard gate.

He goes round the end of the row past a wheelwright's lean-to and comes out onto the main street a few doors below the brass scale. He brushes coal smoke off his sleeves as he walks.

The front of the Scales is as narrow as the back. It has a heavy door with a bell-pull, a step worn hollow in the middle, and one wide ground-floor window with iron bars and thick greenish panes. Behind them he can just make out a counter and the shape of a man bent over it. The brass scale overhead creaks a little as the air stirs. While Pell watches, a broad woman in a smith's leather apron goes in carrying a cloth bundle. The bell inside rings once. A few minutes later she comes out without the bundle and counts something into her palm on the step. Then she walks off toward the forges, frowning, the way people walk away from a moneylender's.

Across the street there's a bakehouse with a bench against its sunny wall, and an old man asleep at the far end of the bench. Pell takes the near end. From here he can see Thole's door, the barred window, and the street back as far as the Red Sheaf, where the step is freshly swept and a groom leads a bay mare into the stable arch. Beyond the inn the street rises and bends. At the top, the carter's dray of staves is backed across the corner by the cooper's yard and hides the mouth of Hesper's lane.

He counts the street the way he'd count a room. There are two carters, a boy with a basket of loaves, a smith's apprentice running an errand, and a woman haggling at the chandler's door. Nobody is sitting on a bench but him and the old man. Nobody stands about, and nobody so much as glances at the Scales except the people going in. In the quarter hour he's sat there, nobody else has gone in at all.

Bram and Sefa haven't come round the bend yet.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I give Wat a small nod. “You needn’t go anywhere with me.”

I move a few paces back toward the lane, giving him and Sefa more room while keeping her in sight. I watch the main street, particularly toward the Red Sheaf where he glanced, and leave her to answer his request.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa holds his look a moment, then nods once, slow.

"Wat. All right." She reaches into her belt-pouch, not the coin purse, and shows him a silver between two fingers, held low by her side where the street can't read it. "A silver, then, for a silver's worth of talk. You stay by your trough, I'll stay here, and the big man stays where he is. If you want to break off, you walk; I won't follow, and I won't call after you."

She tucks the silver back into her fist, but doesn't put it away.

"Swear it how? I won't tell the widow, the moneylender, or anyone in town your name or what we speak of, except the two hired with me, who need to know what keeps us out of trouble. I'd have told them something either way; better the truth than a guess. But your name won't leave my teeth, and if it's heard from them, I'll answer for it."

She cocks her head a little.

"We talk here, plain view of the cooper's gate and everyone. And what I want from you is what you've already got paid to watch: the house itself. Not her. So tell me what you see when you watch a house three days, and I'll know whether that silver's honestly yours." She pauses. "Whoever set you here — was it for the house, or for something at it? And have you seen anyone else watch it besides him?" She gestures, small, at the tiefling. "Not a passing cart. A watcher, like you."

scenes.narration:
Bram's nod gets a wary flick of the eyes from Wat and nothing else. Bram walks back a few paces toward the lane, and the boy's shoulders come down a little as he goes.

From where he stands now Bram can see a long way down the main street. The old man has finished sweeping the Red Sheaf's step and gone inside. A groom leads a bay mare in under the stable arch, and the hooves ring hollow on the cobbles. One shutter on the inn's upper floor stands open. Nobody is at it, only a shirt drying on the sill. Further down, past the inn, the street climbs toward the bend. A sunny bench against a bakehouse wall has two shapes on it, too far off to make out. Nobody is coming up the street, and nobody leaves the Sheaf in a hurry.

At the trough, Wat looks at the silver between Sefa's fingers. Then he looks at her face. The tips of his ears go red.

"Them two, and nobody else," he says. "Not the widow. Not Thole. Not him at the Sheaf." He stops short, as if he's heard himself, and looks back down at the water. "Nobody."

He scrubs one forearm, slowly.

"The house? There's nothing to see. Shutters shut all day. Coal man came the first morning. She went out the day before yesterday, up toward the temple end, by herself, and came back before the bell, walking fast. Yesterday a boy brought her a paper. One of Thole's, he runs for him. She took it at the door and shut it." He shrugs. "Nobody comes to her. Then you lot."

He jerks his chin at the house without looking.

"Three of you went in. Two came out." He says it flatly, the way he'd say a horse threw a shoe. "That's what I'm paid for. Counting."

Then he answers the other thing she asked, more slowly, as if he's making sure he gives her nothing extra.

"Not the house. Her. Who goes in to the widow, what they look like, how many. And if anybody comes out carrying anything, a box or papers or a bundle, I'm to say so special." His eyes come up to hers. "Nobody's carried nothing. Not yet."

He tips his head toward the cooper's wall.

"Him? He's no watcher. He knocked on Dobb's gate yesterday. Dobb's girl told him come back tomorrow and shut it on him. He's been stood there since, working himself up to knock again." He nearly smiles, then thinks better of it. "Nobody else watches. Just me. I'd have seen."

He wipes his hands on his shirt, glances once down the street toward the Sheaf, and holds out his palm, low by his hip where the street can't see it.

"That's a silver's worth. That's all I've got."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell buys a roll from the bakehouse when the boy with the basket comes past, pays copper, and eats it slowly on the bench like a man with nowhere he needs to be. It gives his hands something to do and his face a reason to be pointed at the street.

*Three storeys, taller than either neighbour, strongroom in the back corner with new stone round it. A dog on a chain in the yard, a woman in a cap on the second floor, a cook's fire going. Chandler's roof runs flush — that's the way up, if a way up were ever wanted. It isn't. Not today.* He files it anyway, the way he files everything.

The thing that nags him isn't the Scales. It's the dray of staves backed across the corner up by the cooper's, sitting just where it hides the mouth of Hesper's lane from this whole stretch of street. A carter unloading would have moved it by now. He watches it for the quarter hour — whether anyone's actually working it, whether the dusty tiefling is still leaning on the cooper's wall beside it, whether a boy with bare arms shows at the corner.

When Bram's shield and Sefa's grey come round the bend from the Red Sheaf, he doesn't wave and doesn't rise at once. He lets them get within a few doors of the brass scale, finishes the roll, dusts his fingers, and crosses the street at an angle so that he arrives at Thole's step a pace behind them — a third customer who happens to be going in at the same time.

Quiet, for them only, as Bram reaches for the bell-pull: "Strongroom's the back corner, ground floor, no window, new stone. There's a dog in the yard the size of a pony and a woman upstairs who leans out of windows. Well?" — a look at Sefa — "did the boy talk?"

scenes.narration:
The boy with the basket is working his way down the bench side of the street. Pell lifts a finger, and the boy stops and holds the basket out. The loaves are hot enough that the cloth over them steams. "Copper," the boy says. Pell gives him one. He takes a roll with a brown, floury crust, and the boy moves on toward the chandler's woman without looking back. The old man at the far end of the bench doesn't wake.

Pell eats it slowly and watches the corner.

The dray is being worked, just not quickly. The carter stands up on the bed and hands staves down in armfuls to a lad in a cooper's apron, who carries them in through the yard gate. Each trip takes as long as it takes. Twice the carter stops, leans on the load and says something down to the lad, and the lad laughs. It's the pace of men paid by the load, not by the hour. Nobody else goes near the dray.

From down here the people at the corner are only shapes. Pell can tell where the wall is by the pale stone. A dark figure stands against it, and that would be the tiefling's coat. There's movement on the main-street side, by the trough, but at this distance he can't tell one shape from another. The dray hides the mouth of the lane, the same as before.

About ten minutes in, the cooper's gate opens wider than the lad needs. A girl in a headscarf comes out, and the dark figure comes off the wall to meet her. They stand close together for a moment. Then the girl steps back, holds the gate, and the tiefling goes in through it. The gate shuts behind them both. A while later the lad comes back out alone for another armful.

Closer to the bench, the door of the Scales opens. A boy of ten or eleven comes out with a folded paper. He's narrow, dressed in a clean shirt too good for a stable, and his hair is wetted flat. He jumps the hollow step and trots up the street with the paper held flat against his chest. He doesn't go far. He turns in at the Red Sheaf, past the groom and under the stable arch, and goes inside. Pell finishes his roll. A few minutes later the boy comes out with empty hands and trots back down to the Scales. He doesn't use the bell-pull, just lifts the latch and lets himself in like someone who lives there.

Nobody else goes into the moneylender's.

Near the end of the quarter hour the carter hands down the last armful, jumps off the bed and takes the horse's head. The dray rolls forward out of the corner and turns down toward the forges, and the mouth of Hesper's lane opens up again. Pell can see the cooper's wall, now with no one leaning on it, the trough, and the people beside it. They're still too far off to be more than shapes.

Bram and Sefa haven't come down the street yet.

*(Out of game: Bram and Sefa's scene at the trough is still running, so Pell's crossing to Thole's step waits until they actually come round the bend.)*

Once they do, Pell crosses and speaks exactly as you wrote it.)*

messages.text:
I stay where I am and let Sefa finish, making no sign at Wat’s mention of the third person. No sense teaching him which part worries us.

I take note of the Red Sheaf’s stable arch and open upper window, then return to watching the street. Once Sefa steps away from the trough, I’m ready to walk with her toward the Scales.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:

He doesn't look away from you now, though his eyes slide once toward the main street and back, quick as a heartbeat. He's waiting to see if you mean to pay, and whether the pair of you leave after.

Near the cooper's gate, the tiefling shifts his weight onto his other foot and looks through you both with the fixed, studied expression of a man trying not to be the third part of someone's business.

The water in the trough shivers. Somewhere along the main street a dog starts up at a cart and is quiet again.

Bram stays where he is and keeps his face still. Wat said "two came out" and Bram gives no sign that the number matters. He looks down the main street to the Red Sheaf, at the stable arch where the groom took the bay mare in, and at the open upper shutter with the shirt drying on the sill. Nobody stands at that window, and nobody stands under the arch.

While he watches, a boy comes up the street from the temple end at a trot. He's narrow, ten or eleven, in a clean shirt too good for a stable, with his hair wetted flat. He holds a folded paper flat against his chest. He turns in under the Sheaf's stable arch without slowing and disappears inside. After a short while he comes out again with empty hands and trots back the way he came, down past the inn and out of sight round the bend. Bram doesn't know the boy. Wat's eyes follow him the whole way down the street and come back to Sefa only once he's gone.

Behind them the cooper's gate opens wider than the lad unloading staves needs. A girl in a headscarf steps out. The tiefling comes off the wall to meet her, and for a moment they stand close and talk too low to hear. Then she holds the gate for him, and he goes in with his tail tucked tight and his shoulders up round his ears, like a man finally going to collect what he's owed. The gate shuts behind them both. Up on the dray the carter hands down the last armful of staves, jumps off the bed and takes the horse's head. The dray rolls off down the main street toward the forges.

Wat's palm is still out, low by his hip, and still damp.

I leave Sefa to settle with Wat and walk slowly toward the Scales, keeping within sight so she can catch up. As I pass the Red Sheaf, I give the stable arch an ordinary traveller’s glance without stopping or going inside.

Once Sefa joins me and we’re out of Wat’s hearing, I quietly mention the clean-shirted boy, the paper he delivered under the arch, and how closely Wat watched him. “Might be nothing. Worth telling Pell.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa lets her hand drop open just enough, and curls her fingers once as if taking a coin instead of giving it. "Not just talk."

She passes the silver into his damp palm without touching him, so that from the street it looks like a hand resting at a child's side, and folds her own back into her sleeve.

"That was an honest count, and a silver's worth." She keeps her voice down. "You'll hear no name of yours from me, or from him. To Widow Vallow, to Thole, to anyone at the Sheaf — you were just a boy at a trough. If I ever need to say more, I'll break my own rule before I let it fall on you, and that's harder to do than it sounds."

She half-turns from the trough, as if to end it, then stops, still not blocking his way.

"One more thing, and it's only if you want the earning of it." She produces the second silver between two fingers, low at her side, but doesn't offer it yet. "I won't ask who set you here, and I won't ask why. But a boy went under the Sheaf's arch just now with a paper, out of a good house by the look of him, and went back the way he came. You followed him with your eyes like you knew his business." She pauses. "If you can say, without touching any name — whose paper and what sheaf it's feeding — that's worth another silver to me. And if you can't, or won't, you're still paid for what you said."

She lets that hang, her weight still off the street-side, ready to let him go.

"Either way, Wat: mind the wheel-ruts when the carter comes back, and don't sit with your back to Dobb's gate if his girl takes against you. The hog's pen at the Red Sheaf is a better place to look idle, if you ever need one." The last is almost gentle, no mock in it.Wat's hand closes over the silver. He palms it into his shirt and studies your face while you speak; at the end he looks down the street toward the Sheaf and then back at you. The red has gone out of his ears. It gives his face a closed, older look, the uncertain edge worn off by the simple fact of being paid.

He glances toward Bram, who is still some way off by the lane-mouth, watching the main street as if he'd forgotten all about the pair of you. Then he speaks low and fast, from the corner of his mouth, a boy used to giving a report without moving his head.

"That's Master Corven Ashby's clerk's boy. He's run paper from Ashby to Thole twice since I've been at this trough." A small pause. "Or from someone in the Sheaf to Thole. It goes there and back. I don't know which way."

He looks at the water, at the scum of ash and chaff that has gathered by the trough's lip, and says more slowly, "But I know what Ashby looks like. He came out of the Sheaf the day before yesterday at dusk. A black coat, a gold chain, and a man with him I didn't like. They went in at Thole's door and came out a long time after, past the watch-lanterns." A longer pause. "The widow was already back from the temple end. Somebody writes her paper too, when they want her to know."

He rubs a knuckle under his nose and looks up at you sidelong.

"The boy's master's paper? I don't know what's in it. I don't read words." He says it without shame. Then, quieter, as if it costs him more, "But it went to the Scales, if your man at the counter needs to know it. And that's worth every copper of the other silver, whether you give it me or not."

He holds out no hand this time. He gives a quick, almost scared look past you, up the lane to where the widow's door still stands shut; then he turns sidelong to the trough, shoulders set, ready to go back to watching the house behind you and be not-Wat again.

Where you are: at the trough with Wat, near the cooper's gate · Time: Day 1 · morning

scenes.narration:
Sefa's hand opens at her side and the silver goes into Wat's damp palm without their fingers touching. He shuts his fist on it and pushes it down inside his shirt, all in one movement. He listens to the rest without looking at her. When the second silver shows between her fingers, his eyes go to it and stay there a moment.

"That's Thole's boy," he says, low. "Same one brought the widow her paper yesterday. He's no good house. He sleeps over Thole's counting-room." He scrubs a thumb along the trough's lip. "Paper went in at the Sheaf. To somebody lodging there. Who, I'm not saying. That's as good as a name, and you said no names."

He looks at the second silver again, and then away from it.

"Keep it. That's not a silver's worth, that's half of one." He says it flatly, like he's settling a bill. Then he hears the last thing she said. His head comes round, quicker than he means it to. "There's no pen at the Sheaf. Pigs went at Midwinter." He shuts his mouth, and a moment later he sits back on the trough rim with his back to her and his eyes on the lane.

---

Bram walks off slowly down the main street, the shield easy on his arm. It's the pace of a man with an errand and no hurry. As he passes the Red Sheaf he glances in under the stable arch the way any traveller looks at a stable. It's a cobbled yard. The groom is wisping down the bay mare in the end stall, and an outside stair runs up to a gallery of rooms on the yard side, all their doors shut. A cat is washing itself on the mounting block. The groom looks up, nods at the chain mail the way grooms nod at anyone who might want a horse, and goes back to the mare. Nobody else is in the yard. Bram doesn't stop.

Four doors on, the brass scale creaks over Thole's door. Across the street the sunny bench outside the bakehouse has one occupant, the old man asleep at the far end. The near end is empty. Nobody crosses the street to fall in a pace behind Bram. Nobody turns up on Thole's step. Pell said he would find them, and so far he hasn't.

Sefa catches him up a little short of the hollowed step. Wat and the trough are well behind her, out of hearing. Bram tells her quietly about the boy in the clean shirt: the paper held flat to his chest, the trip in under the Sheaf's arch and out again with empty hands, and how Wat's eyes followed him all the way down the street. He says it might be nothing and is worth telling Pell.

The bell-pull hangs beside Thole's door. Behind the thick green panes of the barred window the shape of a man is still bent over the counter, much as it was earlier.

*(Out of game: I read the lines you gave Wat as a suggestion and played him from what he actually knows. He wouldn't take the second silver for what he gave.)*

 *(Out of game: none of these needed a roll, and all four happened last turn. Bram's word to Sefa and his glance under the arch are plain talk and a caravan guard's routine look, and Sefa's payment, her second offer and her advice were hers to make; Wat refused the second silver himself, from his own sense of fair.)*

He palms it into his shirt and studies your face while you speak; at the end he looks down the street toward the Sheaf and then back at you. The red has gone out of his ears. It gives his face a closed, older look, the uncertain edge worn off by the simple fact of being paid.

He glances toward Bram, who is still some way off by the lane-mouth, watching the main street as if he'd forgotten all about the pair of you. Then he speaks low and fast, from the corner of his mouth, a boy used to giving a report without moving his head.

"That's Thole's boy," he says, low. "Same one brought the widow her paper yesterday. He's no good house. He sleeps over Thole's counting-room." He scrubs a thumb along the trough's lip. He looks at the second silver again, and then away from it.

scenes.narration:
The bell jangles somewhere deep in the house. Behind the green panes the bent shape at the counter straightens. A moment later the latch lifts from inside and the door opens a hand's width. It's the runner boy, the narrow one in the clean shirt with his hair wetted flat. He looks up at Bram's chain mail, then at the shield, then at Sefa, and his hand stays on the door.

Bram gives his name, Sefa's and Hesper's, says what they've come about, and holds up the folded note.

The boy's eyes go to the paper and back to Bram's face. "Master," he calls over his shoulder, not loudly. Then he opens the door all the way and steps back against the wall to let them by.

Inside it's cool and smells of brass polish and old wool. A long counter of dark wood runs across the room. A balance stands on it with its pans level, and there's a row of weights in a velvet-lined box. Behind the counter, shelves go up to the ceiling, full of pledges with paper tickets tied to them on string: a fiddle, a pair of riding boots, a smith's hammer, three candlesticks, and a cloth bundle on the lowest shelf whose knot is still fresh. A door at the back is fitted with an iron grate, and beyond it a dimmer room has a desk and a lamp burning in daylight.

The man at the counter is about fifty. He's lean and close-shaven, and his sleeves are pinned back from the wrist so they won't drag through the ink. He has a pair of Gondish spectacles pushed up on his forehead. He doesn't come round the counter.

"Gaspar Thole." His voice is soft and dry, pitched to carry exactly as far as the counter. He holds out his hand for the note. When Bram gives it to him, he unfolds it, lowers the spectacles and reads it all, top to bottom. Then he reads the last line a second time, with his finger under it. *They may not agree to any sum on my behalf.* He folds it in three along its creases and lays it on the counter between them, squared to the edge.

"Mistress Vallow writes a careful hand." He lifts the spectacles again and looks at Bram first, then a little longer at Sefa, as if trying to place her. "You may hear my terms, Master Halloway. They are the same ones I gave the lady, twice. She won't like them any better from you."

He opens a heavy ledger at a ribbon, turns it a quarter so they can see it's a ledger and not what's written in it, and keeps his palm flat on the page.

"Master Aubrey Vallow pledged one iron coffer, sealed, eight months ago. My book says it is redeemable until sundown this day by the bearer of his ticket, or his lawful heir producing it." He reads that last part off the page word for word, the way a man reads out something he didn't write himself. "Producing it. The lady is his heir. I don't dispute it. But she has no ticket, and without a ticket I have no redemption to offer her, whatever her rights are. What is owed on the ticket I tell to the man who holds the ticket. That is how this house has always been kept."

He closes the ledger on the ribbon.

"At sundown the term lapses. The forfeit passes to the gentleman who bought it." He doesn't say the gentleman's name, though it's on the notice in Bram's coat. "And that is the whole of my terms." His thumb finds the edge of the balance pan and steadies it, though it isn't moving. "If you have questions, ask them. I'll answer what is mine to answer."

The runner boy stays by the wall near the door, listening, his hands behind his back.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I lay Hesper’s note back in its fold and keep my voice as level as his.

“Then the missing ticket is what we must settle, not the sum. If a customer loses one—or dies and his heir cannot find it—does this house accept any lawful substitute? A sworn declaration, a bond against another claimant, an order from a magistrate? Tell us what would satisfy you before sundown.”

I pause to let him answer.

“And has anyone already presented Aubrey’s ticket? I’m not asking what they owe.”

I glance toward Sefa. “We’d also like to see the coffer and its seal, without touching either, as you allowed Mistress Vallow to do.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa has said little since the door opened. She lets Bram hold the man's attention, and while Thole reads the note she studies the shop with a healer's eye: the row of pledges, the fresh knots on that cloth bundle, the runner boy's hands folded behind his back, the lit lamp burning in a room that already has daylight. She doesn't touch anything.

When Thole has finished, she takes a half-step forward so her shadow falls on the counter's edge, not on the ledger.

"Master Thole." She gives the name no warmth and no edge. "We understand your terms exactly. You've built this house on them, and no one's asking you to change them by force."

Her eyes move to the closed door at the back and rest there a moment before they find him again.

"I'd like to see the coffer, as you showed it to her. Through the grate is fine. I won't put a hand on it, and I won't ask you to open anything. But before any one of us carries a figure back to that lady, I need to see that it's whole, that the seal is the one she described, and that it's sitting where you said it was three days ago."

She pauses, steady.

"You'd be right to ask why a stranger should look at a pledge. Because if that wax has been disturbed between her last visit and now, then this isn't a redemption at all, and we're wasting each other's morning. And because I'd rather settle that here in the light than have to come back after dark." A small pause. "If you won't show me, I'll know that, too."

Then, more gently, almost conversationally: "Is there a fee for the showing, or will you do it as a courtesy to the widow?"

scenes.narration:
Thole lets Bram finish both questions. He doesn't interrupt, and nothing in his face shows he's working anything out. When he answers, he starts with the substitutes.

"A sworn declaration from the heir I cannot take, Master Halloway. A widow will swear to her husband's goods. So would the next claimant, and then I would hold two oaths and one coffer." He lifts one finger from the counter. "A bond against another claimant covers me if a claimant comes. It does not stand in for a ticket. As for magistrates, Beregost has none whose writ reaches a pledge. Contracts in this town are witnessed at the Song of the Morning and argued there. If the temple's court of contracts writes to me that the ticket is lost and that the lady stands as its bearer, I will honour that writing." He pauses for exactly as long as the next sentence needs. "I have done it once before, for a smith's widow, eleven years ago. Whether the brothers will sit on such a matter before sundown is not mine to answer."

"Your second question. No. Nobody has presented Master Vallow's ticket, and nobody has offered to." He looks at Bram a moment longer than he has to. "You are not the first to ask me that this week."

He doesn't say who was.

Then Sefa steps up so that her shadow falls across the edge of the counter, and he turns to her. When she says *if you won't show me, I'll know that too*, his mouth thins.

"You would know that I keep my strongroom shut to strangers, mistress. Nothing more." Then, just as dry: "But a pledge shown whole is to this house's credit, not its cost. There is no fee." He takes a key on a cord from his waistcoat pocket and lifts the counter flap. "You'll stand where I put you, and you'll keep your hands at your sides. Both of you."

The boy by the door doesn't move.

Thole unlocks the grated door. The room behind it is the counting-room, small and windowless, and it explains the lamp: the back shutters are latched, and the only light comes from the flame on the desk. messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I keep my hands clear and step back toward the counter when Thole indicates we’re done.

“Thank you. The temple’s ruling gives us a lawful road to try. Will you put that in writing—that you’ll accept their declaration in place of the ticket, provided it reaches you before sundown? It may save the brothers sending someone here to ask.”

I pause, then add, “Who else asked whether the ticket had been presented?”

My eyes flick toward the counting-room. “And is there already a carrier arranged for the coffer after sundown? If we secure that ruling in time, I’d rather not find we’re chasing a wagon.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa doesn't answer him at once. She is still looking through the grille, at the seal with its thin ring of marks and the clean oblong on the shelf. Then she says, to Thole, without turning round:

"You keep a clean strongroom and a steady lamp. You'd notice if a shelf had been disturbed." She pauses. "And yet you're not surprised the flame leans. You've had the chandler at the wick, so I'll take it this isn't the first time. When Mistress Vallow saw the coffer three days ago, did it do the same — and did she remark on it?"

She turns her head a little, not her body, so Thole is still in the edge of her sight.

"And the ring of marks round the sun. Fine writing. Can you read any of it, yourself? Not at the grille, I mean. When it was pledged." Her voice is calm, matter-of-fact.

She keeps her hands at her sides, as told. She doesn't lean toward the gate.

"You are a careful man, I think. You'd have set a candle behind the wax, once, out of ordinary curiosity." A small pause. "What did you make of it?"

scenes.narration:
Thole doesn't answer at once. He backs out of the counting-room, keeping the lamp low at his side, and waits for the two of them to come out ahead of him. Then he pulls the grated door shut and turns the key. Only after that does he look at Bram. The flame leans toward the strongroom wall the whole time, even through the bars.

"In writing." He goes round behind the counter and lifts the flap down. "Yes. It costs me nothing to write down what I have already said. That is the point of saying it."

He takes a half-sheet from under the counter, dips a pen and writes without stopping to think. He turns it round for Bram to read:

*Gaspar Thole, at the sign of the Scales, will honour a writing of the court of contracts of the Song of the Morning that declares Master Aubrey Vallow's pledge ticket lost and names his widow as its bearer, if it is presented at this counter before sundown this day. The sum owed will then be named to her. — G. Thole.*

He sands it, shakes it, and slides it across with Hesper's note.

"Your second question." His voice stays exactly as soft as before. "A man who has paid for a forfeit wants to know whether the pledge will be redeemed. He asked what a buyer would ask. You may take from that what you like."

When Bram says *carrier*, Thole's eyes go to the grated door, past it to the lamp on the desk, and come back. It takes less than a breath.

"What leaves my house after sundown is the buyer's to carry. I don't hire his wagons, and I don't ask where they go." He sets the lamp down on the counter. "What happens to a thing once it is off my shelf isn't my business."

Then he turns to Sefa. She has asked him three things without turning round, and he answers all three to her profile.

"The lady saw it lean. She looked at it a long while and didn't remark on it. I didn't remark on it either."

"The marks I can't read. They're not any letters I keep accounts in."

He's quiet for a moment, and when he goes on it's a little slower, as if he's checking each word before he lets it go.

"You're right about the candle. The day Master Vallow set it on this counter I held one behind the wax. The flame bent to it then, as it bends now. I asked him what the seal was. He said it would keep, and that it wouldn't thank me for handling it." Thole looks at his own hands on the counter. "The wax was warm that morning. That was in the first week of the year, and the iron under it was cold as the street. I wrote *sealed* in my book. Since then I have lifted that coffer by its straps and nothing else."

He doesn't say what he made of it, and it's clear he won't.

Over by the door the runner boy hasn't moved, but he's stopped pretending not to listen.

"You have my writing and your lady's," Thole says. "Is there anything else?"

 *(Out of game: all four happened last turn and none needed a roll, because they were plain questions put honestly and Thole answered each one in the scene: he wrote the undertaking, said the other asker was "a buyer", said the carrier is the buyer's business and not his, and said Hesper saw the flame lean and didn't remark on it.)*

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I read Thole’s undertaking and tuck it safely beside Hesper’s papers.

“One last thing: which brother handles these petitions at the temple?”

Once he answers, I thank him and head outside with Sefa.

“We’ve a way forward without breaking locks. Let’s find Pell, then take this to the Song of the Morning. They may know the seal as well as the law.”

Outside, I step clear of the doorway and look for Pell without calling his name. Quietly to Sefa: “That runner by the door is the boy I saw delivering the paper at the Sheaf.”

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa turns from the grate as Thole locks it, and folds her hands loosely in front of her. She watches him write the note for Bram, then meets his look.

"One other thing, Master Thole, since we're putting down honest words this morning." She says it without challenge. "The coffer's straps. You said you've lifted it by those and nothing else. Are they worn, new, or patched? If you had to guess by the feel of them when you set it on the shelf — is it heavier than it looks, or balanced wrongly? A man who keeps a strongroom sometimes knows more about a thing from putting it away than from looking at it."

She keeps her hands where he can see them and lets the question end there. Then she inclines her head a little toward Bram.

"After that, I think we've taken enough of your morning. We'll carry your writing to the temple, and if the brothers rule, we'll be back before sundown. If not, you'll know it's gone to the buyer fair."

She doesn't say Ashby's name. The runner boy is still listening, and she lets him hear only what a careful woman would say in a shop with ears in it.

scenes.narration:
Thole hears Bram's question and takes a moment before he answers.

"There's no brother at the door who takes them, Master Halloway. A petition to the court of contracts is written into the archive's roll first, and the court sits on what's in the roll when the dawnmaster calls it to sit." He lays the pen down in its tray. "Eleven years ago the smith's widow's petition was written in by the archivist, Sister Maudra Kell. I believe she still keeps the rolls. She is not quick." He adds the next part in the same dry voice. "And the petition is the widow's. It goes in under her name, and she puts her hand to it herself. The court won't hear agents on a matter of an heir's right."

Then he turns to Sefa. He looks at her a little longer this time, as if her question is a better one than he expected.

"The straps are newer than the iron. Good oiled leather, hardly worn, and the buckles are still bright. He had them put on for carrying, I'd say, not for keeping." He pauses over the next part. "As for the weight, it weighs what that much iron weighs and very little more. It doesn't shift when it's tilted. Nothing slides in it and nothing knocks. Whatever is inside, it's packed close, or there isn't much of it." He stops there. "That is what I know from putting it away. I'll not guess further."

When Sefa says *gone to the buyer fair*, his mouth shows nothing. He inclines his head a fraction to each of them.

"Good morning to you both."

The runner boy is already at the door. He opens it for them and stands back against the wall, and his eyes follow them out the way Wat's followed him up the street. On the counter behind them the lamp burns steadily, and its flame still leans toward the counting-room.

---

The door shuts behind them, and the morning is loud again after the shop: hammers from the forges, a cart, and the brass scale creaking overhead. Bram steps down off the hollow step and moves to one side of the doorway, out of the line of the green window, and looks the street over without calling anyone's name.

Across the way the bench outside the bakehouse has the old man asleep at the far end. The near end is empty. Down toward the Red Sheaf there's the swept step, the stable arch and the shirt still drying on the upper sill. Up the street toward the temple end, carters, a woman with a basket and two apprentices argue over a handbarrow. Above the roofs the bell-tower of the Song of the Morning stands pale in the sun. Pell isn't on the bench, at either corner, or anywhere Bram can see along the street. Nobody comes across to fall in a pace behind them.

Bram keeps his voice down, for Sefa only. He tells her the boy by Thole's door is the same runner he watched carry the paper in under the Sheaf's arch.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I speak quietly to Sefa, clear of the shop window.

“Hesper must sign the petition herself. Best fetch her now rather than spend an hour at the temple only to be sent back. She should bring whatever proves she’s Aubrey’s heir.”

I glance along the street once more. “Would you wait here a little for Pell, then meet us at the temple? Tell him about the undertaking and the runner. I’ll bring Hesper—and explain that we’ve promised no money.”

Unless Sefa has an objection, I head back toward Hesper’s house at a purposeful walk, keeping the papers secure.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa steps out of the doorway's shadow and stands where the creaking scale doesn't throw its shadow over either of them. Her voice stays low, for Bram's ear alone.

"I know. Wat told me the paper went to the Sheaf before I paid him. To somebody lodging there is all he'd say." She watches the runner boy's silhouette recede behind the green panes. "So we've a boy who runs between Thole and Ashby's rooms, and a moneylender who won't grant the widow more than a writing. One of these is listening; the other is buying."

She turns her shoulder to the shop and glances along the street, settling on the empty near end of the bakehouse bench.

"We should move off the step before our return is noted at a higher desk. Pell'll find us by now, but he won't slink up while we're framed in this door."

She starts them toward the patch of sun past the shop-front, casual as two people parting from a counter.

"At the temple we'll need Hesper herself for the roll. It's her hand on the petition; the brothers won't hear agents. So we go to the Song first — see if Sister Maudra Kell will set the rolls in motion before the bells ring noon — then back to the house for her mark. It leaves the coffer unwatched for a while." She looks at Bram sidelong. "Unless Pell's made friends with the cooper's girl and the whole street's been cast for us already."
