messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Fair enough. Temple first, together. If there’s a delay, we’ll use it to fetch Hesper.”

I fall into step beside Sefa toward the Song of the Morning. “Thole’s writing again, with his runner waiting. We should assume Ashby will hear what we asked. Nothing to be done about that by standing here.”

I keep an eye out for Pell as we walk, but don’t stop to search.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
"Fetch her, then." Sefa nods once, already turning toward the empty patch of wall at the side of the baker's, where the sun lies and the bench end is clear. "I'll give Pell a short while here. If he comes, I'll bring him up to the temple with me; if he doesn't, I'll walk up alone and find Sister Maudra before the noon bell. The two of us can be inside getting a sense of the rolls while you and Hesper are still on the lane."

She pauses before he goes.

"Lord Halloway — when you tell her we promised no money, tell her also no one at the Scales has said the full sum or offered it. And mind the boy at the trough. He's been bought to watch her, and he's just watched you." She doesn't say this loudly. "He may run ahead of you. If you see him move before you pass the Red Sheaf, cross the street and come up the temple side with her. I'll keep an eye from here until you're past the stable arch."

Then she sets her back to the green window, out of its sight-line, and lets the street be loud.

scenes.narration:
Bram says his piece and turns toward the temple end, ready to walk with Sefa. Thole is writing again with his runner waiting beside him, he says, so they should assume Ashby hears what they asked. Standing here won't change that.

Sefa is already turning the other way, toward the sunny wall by the bakehouse. She heard Bram's plan from the last turn and has come round to it at the same moment he came round to hers. "Fetch her, then." She'll give Pell a little while here, she says, and go up to the temple alone if he doesn't come.

So they stand two paces apart on the cobbles, each set on the other's plan. A carter passes between them, sees nothing odd in it and drives on.

Sefa finishes anyway, low and plain. Hesper should hear that nobody at the Scales named a sum or offered one. And the boy at the trough was paid to watch the widow, and he has just watched Bram. If Wat moves before Bram is past the Red Sheaf, Bram should cross and come up the temple side of the street with Hesper. Then she steps back against the wall, out of the green window's line, as if she's already been left on watch.

Behind her the door of the Scales opens.

The runner boy comes out with a folded paper held flat to his chest, the way he did an hour ago. He jumps the hollow step without looking at either of them and trots down the street, toward the swept step and the stable arch of the Red Sheaf four doors down. Through the green panes, Thole has gone back to his ledger.

Pell is nowhere on the street.

*(Out of game: you've swapped plans. Bram is now set on going to the temple together and Sefa on Bram fetching Hesper, so Bram hasn't walked anywhere yet. Settle which it is, and say whether either of you does anything about the runner.)*

Bram doesn't call after the runner. He turns his back on the Scales and sets off down the street at a working pace. Sefa stays by the bakehouse wall, out of the green window's line.

The runner is four doors ahead and running, and he gets to the Red Sheaf first. When Bram passes the stable arch a few breaths later, the boy is already halfway up the outside stair to the gallery, the paper still flat against his chest. Bram only gives it the glance a man gives any inn yard. Up on the gallery a door opens a hand's width. A hand takes the paper and the door shuts again. The boy turns round on the stair. The groom is still working on the bay mare. Bram keeps walking.

Past the Sheaf the street climbs and bends, and the cooper's corner comes into view. Wat is still on the rim of the trough, exactly where they left him, his forearms dry now. He doesn't get up and he doesn't leave. When Bram comes round the corner alone and turns into the lane, the boy's head comes round, a little slower than this morning, and it stays turned. Wat watches him all the way to the widow's door. Bram can feel the boy counting him.

He knocks and gives his name through the oak, then says the rest: there's a lawful way to redeem the coffer, but the temple needs her there in person.

The bolt slides back. Hesper opens the door just wide enough for him to come in. When he's inside she shuts it and bolts it again. In the brown dimness of the hall she doesn't ask him to sit.

"In person." She says it the way a clerk repeats a clause to make sure it's been copied right. "Thole told you so, or the temple?"

She doesn't wait for the answer before she asks the next thing, just as level.

"Did he name a sum?"

Then she looks past Bram at the bolted door, as if Sefa and Pell might be standing on the step behind him.

"And the other two. Where are they?"

She folds her ink-stained hands, then unfolds them, and says the rest before he can start.

"Our marriage lines were witnessed at the Song of the Morning. They have my name already, so that much is no secret from them. I'll come, and I'll put my hand to a petition." The next part is slower. "But the petition is about a ticket, Master Halloway. A lost ticket and a widow's right. It says nothing about what's pressed into the wax on that coffer, and neither do we while we're there. That is my condition. Do you understand it?"

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Thole told us. He’s put in writing that he’ll accept the temple court’s declaration naming you bearer of the lost ticket, if we bring it before sundown.” I show her his undertaking. “No sum named, none offered, and no payment promised.”

“Sefa is waiting briefly for Pell, then going to find Sister Maudra Kell at the temple. Pell hadn’t rejoined us when I left.”

I give her a moment to read.

“The petition is about your right to redeem the pledge. I won’t volunteer anything about the seal. But if the court asks a direct question, I won’t lie to get its ruling.”

I tuck the paper away once she’s finished. “Bring any papers that establish your marriage and inheritance. One question before we go: is there a danger in mentioning that seal? You needn’t explain its secrets, but I need to know if we’re putting someone at risk.”

scenes.narration:
Hesper takes Thole's half-sheet over to the strip of light by the shutter and reads it once, quickly, the way she'd read a clause she has drafted herself. Her lips move on one word near the end: *bearer*.

"Before sundown," she says. She hands it back and watches him put it away.

Then she answers him, in order.

"Thole, then. Not the temple. Good. He's put it in writing, so he can't take it back." She doesn't comment on the sum, only nods once at *none offered*. At the news about the other two her eyes go to the bolted door again. "Mistress Marrin goes ahead to the archive. And Master Dunmore has my purse and hasn't come back." She doesn't make anything of it. She just says it, like a figure entered in a column.

When Bram says he won't lie to the court, she looks at him a little longer than before.

"I haven't asked you to lie, Master Halloway. I asked you not to bring it up. If the court asks you about the seal, you tell them there's a seal on a coffer at Thole's, and that it's mine to answer for, not yours. Then you let me answer."

His last question takes her a moment. She goes to the desk in the front room and opens a drawer, and while she talks she lifts papers out and sorts them on the blotter without looking at them much.

"Danger. I don't know. That's the honest answer, and you'd know if I gave you a different one." She squares a folded sheet on top of the pile. "The mark on that wax is a sun. Anyone in this town knows whose sun that is. If it belongs to the Song of the Morning, they'll want it back, and a widow's petition about a lost ticket turns into the temple's business about its own property. I'd never see the coffer again." She pauses, and goes on just as level. "And Aubrey carried it out of this house in the first week of the year, and a month later he was lying at the foot of their steps. I'm not saying those two things are connected. I'm saying I don't know that they aren't, and until I do, I won't put that wax in front of them."

She ties the papers with a length of tape.

"My copy of our marriage lines, witnessed at the Song. Aubrey's will, which leaves me everything. It's short, he never cared for long ones." Then she lifts one more slip from the drawer and holds it a moment before she adds it to the bundle. It's a small square of temple paper, stamped with a sunburst. "The archive's receipt. Aubrey lodged the sealed copy of his will there himself, last autumn. I'd forgotten I had this." She turns it so Bram can read the signature at the bottom, in a cramped, careful hand: *M. Kell, archivist.*

She puts on a grey bonnet from the peg in the hall and ties it under her chin, and takes up the bundle.

"I'm ready." She stops with her hand near the bolt and looks back at him. "The boy will be at the trough. Do we go out the front, where he can count us, or the back?"

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa stayed by the bakehouse wall, letting the warmth of the stones soak through her coat. She hooked her thumbs in her belt, the prayer beads slack at her wrist, and let the street move past her. The hammers from the forges had settled into a steady four-beat somewhere below, and every now and again the brass scale over Thole's door creaked when the wind or a passing cart disturbed the air. She listened to that creak and did not turn toward it.

The runner was out of sight. Bram too.

She touched the beads with the heel of her thumb, the old shape-counting comfort, and mouthed a half-heard hospice verse that asked for nothing in particular. *Keep the hours, keep the lamps, keep the watcher.* Then she let her eyes travel the length of the street: the temple bell-tower pale above the roofline, the apprentices still cursing each other as they muscled the handbarrow out of a doorway, the old man deep asleep at the far end of the bakehouse bench with his chin on his chest and a fly walking along the brim of his hat. Nothing closed on her, and no one bobbed out of the traffic looking for a fight or a purse. There was only the ordinary mechanics of a trade morning, and the slow, visible lowering of a mercantile sun.

A woman came out of the bakehouse with three loaves wrapped in cloth, passed so close Sefa could smell the fresh flour off her, and asked, not unkindly, whether she was waiting for someone. Sefa shook her head with an easy half-smile.

"In—no. Only letting the shadow move past." The woman gave a small nod, bewildered at the answer, and went off up the street with her loaves.

Sefa watched her to the corner. Then she returned her eyes to the mouth of the lane by the Red Sheaf, the way Bram had gone, and to the windows of the Sheaf itself, four doors down, where a shirt hung wet and idle from an upper sill and told no tales at all. She measured the bell-shadow on the cobbles, checked the position of the old man on the bench once more, and went on waiting.

scenes.narration:
The sun climbs over Beregost. The shadow of the bell-tower lies across the cobbles toward the bakehouse, and it gets a little shorter each time Sefa checks it. Noon is still a good way off. The woman with the loaves gives Sefa's answer a puzzled nod and goes on up the street, and the bench is back to the old man and his fly.

For a few minutes nothing happens. A carter waters his horse at the chandler's step. The apprentices get the handbarrow clear at last and push it off down toward the forges, still arguing. Behind the green panes across the way, Thole's shape is bent over the counter. Pell doesn't come round either corner. Nobody crosses the street to drop onto the empty end of the bench.

Then a man walks out under the Red Sheaf's stable arch.

He isn't the groom, and he isn't the runner. He's somewhere in his thirties, with close-cropped hair and road leathers, worn but well kept. A sword rides his left hip, its grip wrapped in cord gone dark with handling. He stops on the cobbles just long enough to look up the street and down it, the way a man checks the weather. messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“The back. No need to give him an easy report. We’ll take the alley by the forges, then ordinary streets to the temple. Walk beside me.”

I pause before heading down the passage. “I understand your concern about the seal. I won’t raise it.”

At the yard gate, I listen, then open it enough to look along the alley before bringing Hesper through. If the way is clear, I escort her toward the Song of the Morning, avoiding the trough and the Red Sheaf where the streets allow.

scenes.narration:
Hesper's mouth thins at "walk beside me," but she doesn't argue. She offered him the back way herself this morning.

"Good," she says when he tells her he won't raise the seal. That's all she says about it. She follows him down the passage with the bundle under her arm.

The kitchen is as tidy as it was, with the one cup still upturned on the drainboard. Bram lifts the bar, crosses the yard past the woodpile and stops at the gate to listen. He hears the forges below, steady as before, and a cart somewhere on the main street. Nothing moves close by. He lifts the latch and looks along the alley through the gap. The coal smoke lies along it at head height, the cat has gone from its wall, and nobody stands in a doorway or leans from a window. He opens the gate the rest of the way and brings Hesper through. She draws it shut behind her and drops the latch herself, without being asked.

They go down the smoky side together. In the yard behind the two smithies the apprentices have the bar-iron cart unloaded now. One of them is sluicing his head under a pump, and he looks up at the man in chain and the woman in a grey bonnet the way he'd look at anyone passing through, then ducks back under the water. The gap between the forge and the stable lets them out onto the lanes behind the main street.

Bram can smell the Red Sheaf before he sees it: horses, straw, a midden. The first lane would take them right along the back wall of its stable yard. He turns them one lane further back instead, along a path between kitchen gardens where washing hangs in the sun and a woman on her knees among bean rows doesn't bother to look up. It's longer and the ground is rougher. Hesper keeps up and says nothing about it. Where the gardens end, a gap between a wheelwright's and a dyer's lets them back toward the street, well up toward the temple end, with the Sheaf and the Scales somewhere behind them below the bend. Nobody falls in behind them on the way.

The Song of the Morning stands where the main street widens into a paved square. It's built of pale stone that shows rose in the sun, with a broad flight of steps worn hollow in the middle like Thole's doorstep. The great doors at the top stand open on a dim, gold-lit nave, and a smell of incense and candle-wax drifts out over the square. Near the top a lay brother in an undyed tabard is sweeping. Two women come down past him with a child between them, and a carter waits at the foot of the steps holding his hat. To the left a lower range of buildings runs back along the square, with a smaller arched door under a carved sunburst.

At the foot of the steps Hesper stops for a moment. She doesn't look at the doors. She looks at the steps themselves, about a third of the way up. Then she shifts the bundle under her arm and her face goes back to the way it always is.

On the low wall that edges the square, a few yards from the bottom step, a man is sitting alone. He's somewhere in his thirties, with close-cropped hair and road leathers, worn but well kept, and a sword on his left hip whose grip is wrapped in cord gone dark with handling. He has a heel of bread in one hand that he isn't eating. He isn't looking at the temple doors. He's watching the people who go up to them. As Bram and Hesper come out of the gap by the dyer's, his eyes move to them and stay a moment, on the chain mail first and then on the grey bonnet. Then he tears off a piece of bread and looks down at it.

Bram doesn't know him. He has never seen the man before.

I don’t stare back at the man on the wall. I keep beside Hesper and give her the moment she needs at the steps.

“Which way to the archive?” I ask her quietly.

If she knows, I go with her directly there. Otherwise I ask the sweeping brother, “Good morning. Where can we find Sister Maudra Kell? Mistress Vallow needs to lodge a petition, and our companion Sefa Marrin may already be asking for her.”

As we move, I keep the seated man in the edge of my sight, watching whether he rises to follow.

Bram doesn't look at the wall. He waits at the foot of the steps while Hesper looks at the stone a third of the way up. When she shifts the bundle under her arm again, he asks her quietly which way the archive is.

"The low door. Under the carved sun." She doesn't point. "I went in once, twenty-two years ago, for our lines. It hasn't moved."

They cross the square together along the foot of the steps. Bram keeps the man on the wall at the edge of his sight. The man doesn't get up. He tears off another piece of bread, and as they pass he shifts round on the wall, easily, the way a man moves out of the sun. Now he is facing the low range and its arched door. He doesn't watch them go in. He watches the door.

Bram doesn't need the sweeping brother. The arched door stands half open on a short passage that smells of dust and lamp oil, and at its end is a long, low room with a barrel vault. Pigeonholes line both walls from floor to ceiling, each one stacked with rolled parchments, and every roll is tagged. The only daylight comes from two deep windows in the far wall. Under one of them a woman sits at a sloped desk with a roll weighted open in front of her.

She's old, past seventy, small and straight-backed in an undyed habit with a sunburst stitched in faded thread at the breast. She finishes the line she's writing before she looks up. Then she wipes the pen, sets it down in its groove, and only after that does she ask, "Yes?"

Hesper steps forward and gives her name, and says she has come to petition the court of contracts. She lays the archive's receipt on the corner of the desk, the small square of temple paper with *M. Kell, archivist* at the foot.

Sister Maudra looks at the receipt for a long time without touching it.

"Vallow," she says. "Aubrey Vallow's widow." It isn't a question. "And what is the petition, Mistress Vallow?"

Hesper tells her: a pledge at the Scales, a lost ticket, a widow's right, and sundown.

"Lost," Sister Maudra says. She looks at Hesper a while, then says slowly, "It isn't lost."

She gets up, which takes her a moment, and goes to a squat iron-bound press against the wall. She unlocks it with a key from her sleeve and takes out a small folded paper from a drawer inside. It's closed with a plain red wafer, nothing more. She brings it back and sets it on the desk between them. On the outside, in a cramped, careful notary's hand, is written: *For my wife, if it comes to it. A.V.*

Hesper doesn't reach for it. She looks at the handwriting, and for a breath her face isn't the way it always is. Then it is again.

Sister Maudra keeps two fingers resting on the edge of the paper.

"He brought me his will last autumn, and this with it. He asked me to keep it apart from the will and give it only to you." Her voice is level and unhurried. "He asked me something else that day as well. He asked how a certain kind of seal is opened, and I couldn't tell him. Not then." Her eyes go to the bundle under Hesper's arm, then back to her face. "What he pledged at the Scales. Is there a seal on it? Pale wax, with a sun in it?"

"That is mine to answer for, Sister," Hesper says, "and I won't answer it here."

Sister Maudra takes this without any sign of offence. Her fingers stay where they are on the folded paper. Then she turns her head and looks up at Bram, the big man in chain standing a pace behind the widow, the one person in the room who hasn't spoken.

"And you, sir? Have you seen it?"

messages.text:
The quarter hour has gone. The girl's bucket water runs off and dries in streaks along the gutter. The runner has gone back in at the Scales and pulled the door to. No one else has come down from the Sheaf, and Bram is long since past the lane. Pell hasn't come round either corner.

You said you would give him a short while, then walk up to the Song of the Morning alone. That while is now used. The sun is clean on the tower, and the street is as open as it will be all day.

scenes.narration:
Sefa leaves the warm wall and walks up the main street toward the bell-tower, at the pace of a woman with an errand and no reason to hurry. She passes the saddler's, where an apprentice is stitching a girth in the doorway with the leather across his knee. Past that the street is mostly carts. One driver has stopped to argue the price of a hen with a woman at her gate, and the hen sits under one arm and doesn't care. Beregost goes about its morning. Nobody falls in behind her, and nobody comes down the street to meet her.

At the temple end the street opens into the paved square. The Song of the Morning rises at the far side in pale stone that shows rose in the sun. Its great doors stand open at the top of the broad, hollow-worn steps, and the smell of incense and candle-wax drifts out over the square. A lay brother in an undyed tabard is sweeping near the top. A carter waits at the foot of the steps with his hat in his hands. To the left a lower range of buildings runs back along the square, with a small arched door under a carved sunburst. The door stands half open.

There's no grey bonnet and no chain mail anywhere in the square.

On the low wall at the edge of the square, a few yards from the bottom step, sits the man in road leathers. Close-cropped hair, the cord on his sword grip dark with handling. He has a heel of bread in one hand that he isn't eating, and he isn't looking at the temple doors. He has settled himself on the wall facing the lower range, and his eyes are on the half-open arched door.

When Sefa comes out of the street mouth into the open square, his eyes leave the door and find her. On the street below he gave her half a breath, the way you'd look at a cat on a step. This time he looks longer. His gaze goes to the beads at her wrist and back to her face, and stays there a moment, like a man fitting a face to somewhere he's seen it. Then he tears a piece off the bread and turns back to the door.

Sefa stands at the edge of the square in full sun, with the steps ahead of her and the arched door off to her left.

*(Out of game: I've read this as Sefa going up to the temple alone, as she said she would. It's about 10:55. She's stopped at the edge of the square, and what she does next is up to her.)*

scenes.narration:
Sister Maudra listens to Bram without looking away. When he's finished she says nothing for a moment. Her two fingers stay on the edge of the folded paper.

"You've seen it," she says. "And you leave the seal to her." She nods once, as if he had said more than that. "Very well."

She answers his questions in order, slowly, the way she does everything.

"Whether the ticket is in this paper, I can't tell you. I didn't open it. It was closed when he gave it to me, and it's closed now." She turns it a little so the plain red wafer shows, whole. "He set no condition but the one written on it, and the one he said aloud. It was to go to his wife and to nobody else, kept apart from the will, and only if she came for it. He didn't say what *if it comes to it* meant. I didn't ask him." Her eyes go to Hesper. "You've come for it."

She lifts her fingers off the paper and pushes it across the desk to Hesper.

Hesper looks at it a moment longer. Then she picks it up and breaks the wafer with her thumbnail, the way a woman opens a letter she has opened a thousand of. Inside is a second paper, folded small, and around it a sheet in the same cramped hand. She reads the sheet to herself. It's short. Her mouth moves on one word near the end, and then she folds the sheet in half and in half again and puts it inside her coat, against her chest. She doesn't offer it to anyone.

She unfolds the smaller paper and turns it toward the window light so Bram can read it over her shoulder. It's a printed slip with blanks filled in by hand, in the same tidy clerk's writing as the notice in Bram's coat:

*At the sign of the Scales, Beregost. Received of Master Aubrey Vallow, notary: one iron coffer, sealed, in pledge for one hundred and twenty gold. Redeemable by the bearer of this ticket, or his lawful heir producing it, until sundown of the term. — G. Thole.* A small brass stamp in the corner shows a pair of scales.

"One hundred and twenty," Hesper says. That's all she says.

Sister Maudra watches her put the ticket away with the will and the marriage lines, and tie the tape again.

"You have no need of the court now, Mistress Vallow. A ticket in the heir's hand is what Thole's book asks for." She picks up her pen, looks at the nib, and lays it back in its groove without writing. "I'll say one thing that is mine to say, since nobody else in this room will. If the wax on that coffer is pale and has a sun in it, it was made in this house. Not by your husband, and not for him. This house will want to know how it left." She folds her hands on the desk. "I won't come to Thole's counter and take it out of your hands. But I keep the rolls, and I'll write down what I've been told today, and what I haven't. The dawnmaster reads what I write."

Hesper holds the bundle against her coat. Her face has gone back to the way it always is.

"Thank you for keeping it, Sister," she says. "He chose well, giving it to you." Then she turns to Bram, already half toward the passage and the bright square beyond it. "Thole's, then. Before he's had time to send for anyone."

messages.text:
Sefa doesn't return the man's look, but she keeps him at the edge of her sight and doesn't front the square in a way that puts her back to him. She weighs the two doors—the great temple entrance, and the little arched one under the sunburst—and after a breath she chooses the great door first.

The carter at the foot of the steps clutches his hat tighter as she passes, perhaps glad not to be the only one standing idle outside a god's house. Sefa climbs with a greeting to the sweeping brother: an open palm at her hip, then a touch to the inside of the doorpost as she crosses the threshold. It's not a gesture of need, only of coming in clean.

Then she is out of the sun, into the cool of the temple, with the noise of the square behind her like a tide shut behind a door.

Inside, the nave lies in long beams of rose-coloured light, and the air is heavy with beeswax and braziers. The high windows throw crosses of sun onto the stone, and far up at the altar a cloth hangs like a still dawn. A few worshippers are scattered among the benches, no one you know. A boy in lay garments moves along the wall trimming wicks, and one old woman kneels at the rail near the front, mouthing something. From somewhere off to the left, under the crossing, you can hear the soft flap of papers and the low voice of a woman reading.

You pause just inside, your shadow slack on the threshold.

*(Out of game: you are inside; Bram and Hesper have not arrived. You've entered by the main doors. The man in road leathers is watching the little door.)*

Where you are: inside the nave of the Song of the Morning · Time: Day 1 · midday

scenes.narration:
Sefa keeps the man on the wall at the edge of her sight and crosses the square without looking at him. The carter at the foot of the steps grips his hat a little tighter as she passes. She climbs the hollow steps in the sun.

The lay brother near the top stops sweeping as she comes up. He's young and round-faced, with straw in the bristles of his broom, and he sees the open palm at her hip. When her fingers brush the inside of the doorpost his eyebrows go up. It isn't disapproval. He's seen the gesture before, though not often.

"Dawn's blessing, mistress." He says it the way a man says good morning a hundred times a day. Then he looks at her again. "Hospice manners, those. My aunt did that in Nashkel." He goes back to his sweeping and leaves the doorway clear for her.

Inside, the noise of the square falls away. The nave is long and high and cool, and it smells of beeswax and old incense. The east windows throw slanting bars of rose and gold down across the benches and the worn flags. At the far end the altar cloth hangs pale as early light, with a great sunburst of beaten brass above it that catches the sun and holds it. A few people sit scattered on the benches, none of them anyone she knows. A boy in a lay tabard is working along the north wall with a snuffer and a pair of shears, trimming the wicks of the votive candles one by one. Near the front an old woman kneels at the rail, and her lips move without a sound.

The candles the boy hasn't reached yet burn straight up. None of them lean.

On the left, where the nave meets the crossing, a plain door stands ajar in the side wall. Through the gap Sefa can see the start of a stone passage running back toward the lower range outside, the buildings with the arched door under the carved sun. The passage is empty. Nobody is reading aloud and no papers are moving anywhere she can hear. The only sounds are the snip of the boy's shears and the old woman's breathing at the rail.

Behind her, through the great doors, the square is a bright square of noise. From in here she can't see the low wall.

*(Out of game: I've kept your nave apart from the woman reading, who isn't there, and it's about 11:08, not yet midday.)*

 *(Out of game: none of the three needed a roll, and all three happened in the turn. Keeping the man at the edge of her sight while she walks was just watching, choosing the great door was her own call, and the greeting and the touch at the doorpost were ordinary courtesy, which the sweeping brother answered.)*

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Thole’s, then. Have you the money with you? The ticket names a hundred and twenty; we still need his full redemption figure before you approve payment.”

I turn briefly to Maudra. “If Sefa Marrin or Pell Dunmore comes asking for Bram, please tell them we’ve gone to the Scales.”

At the outer door I pause to look across the square, checking for our companions and the man with the bread before stepping out beside Hesper.

Quietly, I add, “There was a swordsman watching arrivals when we came in. He turned to watch this door as we crossed. Do you know him?”

scenes.narration:
"Thole's, then," Hesper says again. She stops in the passage, because Bram has asked her a question and she answers questions.

"No. I haven't brought it." She shifts the bundle under her arm. "I don't carry gold through this town on a hope, Master Halloway. The money is in the house. He names his figure to the ticket, I hear it, and if I agree to it you can walk me home for the coin and back again. The ticket says one hundred and twenty. What he'll say, I don't know." Her mouth thins. "Something more. They always do, the week the term falls due."

Behind them Sister Maudra has picked up her pen again. She doesn't write. When Bram turns back to her she looks up at once this time.

"Sefa Marrin. Pell Dunmore." She says each name as if she's entering it in a roll. "If either comes asking for you, I'll tell them the Scales." She looks down at the page. "Nobody else will hear it from me."

---

The passage is dim, and the square outside is very bright. Bram stops just inside the arched door and lets his eyes get used to the light before he steps out.

The carter has gone from the foot of the steps. The lay brother is still sweeping near the top, slowly, with his back to the square. The great doors stand open on gold-lit dark, and from here Bram can see nothing inside but the first bars of light on the flags. There's no grey coat with beads at the wrist anywhere in the square, and no one with Pell's walk at either street mouth.

The man on the low wall hasn't moved. He's still sitting where the shade of the steps comes nearly to his boots, with the heel of bread in his hand and less of it left than there was. When the arched door darkens with chain mail, his head doesn't turn. His eyes do. They go to Bram, then to the grey bonnet beside him, and then to the bundle under Hesper's arm, and they stay on the bundle a moment longer than on either face. Then he looks at his bread.

Bram steps out into the sun beside her.

He asks her quietly. Hesper doesn't turn her head the way most people would. She settles her bonnet strings, which don't need it, and lets her eyes cross the square on the way back.

"No." She says it at once and flatly. "I've never seen him. Not in the lane, not at Thole's, not at market." Her fingers tighten on the tape round the bundle. "He watched us go in. He watched the door while we were inside. And now he's looking at what I'm carrying." She doesn't say what she makes of it. "The Scales is down the main street. If he means to know where we're going, he only has to stand up."

She waits beside him on the step, the bundle held against her coat, for him to choose the way.

messages.text:
You leave the great doorway and walk down the north side of the nave, past the boy at the candles. He doesn't look round; he has reached the wicks halfway along the wall, and the flame of each candle he takes flutters once and settles. You cross left of the crossing toward the half-open door. Near the front the old woman at the rail is very still. Her lips move, and her hands are open on her knees, palms up to the altar light.

The door on the left stands ajar just enough to let one person through. From where you are now, the passage beyond runs ten or twelve feet to a plain door set flush in the wall, with a slate hanging on it. On the slate, in chalk and a steady hand: *ROLLS AND ARCHIVE. RING.* Under that, smaller: *M. Kell.* A bell-pull of braided red cord hangs beside the reading. There's no dragging sound or paper-shuffle out there now, and no low voice.

The passage is cool close stone, cut back into the wall; at the far end, on the other side, a lancet window tells you there might be a small court or stairwell before the archivist's door. A wedge of daylight lies across the floor, falling from the window onto the last two flags before the door. You can't see the little square through it, only sky and the corner of a cloud. The man in road leathers could be directly beneath that window and you wouldn't know it from here.

You pause just inside the passage, looking back once toward the great doors, then toward the door at the end. You can hear the old woman's lips still stirring against the silence of the nave, and the distant, faint throbbing of a saw somewhere in the town.

Where you are: in the side passage off the nave, before the archive door · Time: Day 1 · midday

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“Main street. Plenty of people, and we’re doing nothing to hide.”

I walk beside Hesper toward the Scales, keeping myself between her and the seated swordsman as we cross the square. I don’t challenge him, but check whether he follows once we reach the street.

At Thole’s, I pull the bell and stay close to Hesper. When we’re admitted, I let her present the ticket herself.

“Mistress Vallow has recovered the ticket. Please give her the full redemption sum, including any charges.”

scenes.narration:
Bram walks Hesper across the square on the side nearest the low wall, so his chain mail is between her and the man with the bread. He doesn't look at him. He doesn't need to. Halfway across, at the edge of his sight, the man brushes the crumbs off his knee and stands up.

They turn down into the main street. Bram doesn't look back. He reads the street behind them the way he'd read a road, in a shop's dark window and from the angle a carter's head turns as someone goes past him. The man in road leathers comes down the far side of the street, a good thirty or forty feet back, at the same long, even stride as before. He doesn't close the gap and he doesn't drop back. When Bram stops on Thole's hollow step and reaches for the bell-pull, the man walks on a few doors, crosses the street, and sits down on the sunny bench outside the bakehouse. He takes the near end, where Pell sat, while the old man sleeps at the other.

The bell jangles inside. Bram waits, and further down the street something else moves. A bare-armed boy comes down from the cooper's corner at a trot, past the Red Sheaf's swept step, and turns in under the stable arch. It's Wat. He's left the trough.

The latch lifts. Thole's runner opens the door, looks up at Bram, then at the grey bonnet, and stands back against the wall without being told.

---

Thole is at the counter with the ledger open, exactly where he was. He looks up at Hesper first and at Bram second. "Mistress Vallow."

Hesper doesn't answer that. She unties the tape on her bundle, takes out the small printed slip and lays it on the dark wood in front of him, the right way up for him to read. She keeps two fingers on its corner.

Thole lowers his spectacles. He reads the ticket once and then a second time. He opens the ledger to its ribbon and lays his finger on an entry, then looks back at the slip, at the hand-written blanks and at the little brass stamp of the scales in the corner. Something goes across his face, too quick for Bram to name, and it's gone.

"That is my ticket," he says. "Written in this house, eight months ago." He doesn't ask where it's been. He pushes the spectacles back up.

Bram says his piece: the full redemption sum, all charges included.

"All of it, then." Thole draws a half-sheet toward him and writes as he talks, a line for each item, in the same soft voice. "Principal on the ticket, one hundred and twenty. Interest at the house's rate for a pledge it may not look inside, a tenth part a month for eight months, ninety-six. Keeping in the strongroom, three a month, twenty-four." The pen stops, then goes on. "And sixty. That's the return of what the gentleman paid for the forfeit, with what the house owes him for not delivering it. A redeemer who takes back a pledge whose forfeit has been sold pays that charge, or the house is out of pocket for keeping its word." He turns the sheet so they can read it. At the bottom, underlined once: *Three hundred gold.*

His thumb goes to the edge of the balance pan and steadies it.

Hesper reads the sheet. She doesn't pick it up. When she speaks it's level, and she takes his items in the order he gave them.

"The principal is on the ticket. I'll pay it." A beat. "The rate isn't on the ticket, but it's over your door, and Aubrey would have read it. I'll pay that." Another beat. "Keeping, the same." Then her finger moves down to the last line and stops beside it, not quite touching.

"This I don't owe. I sold nothing to that gentleman. If you sold him a thing that was never yours to sell until sundown, that is your bargain, Master Thole, and you can make it good yourself." She folds her ink-stained hands on the counter. "Two hundred and forty."

Thole doesn't look at her hands. He looks at the half-sheet.

"Two hundred and forty, mistress, and the coffer stays on my shelf until the term runs out." His voice doesn't rise. "Three hundred, and it goes with you today. That is the whole of it."

Nobody says anything. By the door the runner boy has stopped pretending not to listen. Through the thick green panes, the shape on the bakehouse bench across the street hasn't moved.

 Bram answered Hesper before they left the arched door: "Main street. Plenty of people, and we're doing nothing to hide." She nodded once and kept the bundle against her coat. Then they crossed the square.

*(Out of game: none of the four needed a roll. Bram's line to Hesper is plain speech. Keeping himself between her and the swordsman, and spotting the man following 30 to 40 feet back, then taking the bench, are routine caravan-guard work, and both were played. So were the bell and his staying close to her at the counter.)*

messages.text:
Sefa listens once more at the flush stone door. The pen scratches on, a slow and certain sound, and in the pause between lines she can hear the shift of paper being squared to paper. She breathes out softly, squares her own shoulders, and rings the bell. One pull, not sharp — enough to be polite and no more.

While she waits, she fixes in her mind the two things she means to ask, and the one she does not. The bell sound still hangs in the narrow passage, small and out of place against all that stone.

Then she arranges her face for an archivist: not a patient, not a tradesman, but a woman carrying someone else's lawful business and one question of her own.

scenes.narration:
Sefa pulls the red cord once. Somewhere beyond the door a small bell answers, thin and clear, and the sound runs back down the passage and dies against the stone.

The pen doesn't stop. It finishes its line, unhurried, and only then goes quiet. After a pause a woman's voice comes through the door, level and not loud.

"Come."

The door is heavier than it looks. It swings inward on a long, low room with a barrel vault, and the smell hits her first: dust, lamp oil, old parchment. Pigeonholes climb both walls from floor to ceiling, and every one is stacked with tagged rolls. Daylight comes in through two deep windows in the far wall and lies in two pale slabs across the flags. At the other end of the room a short passage leads off toward a half-open arched door and a strip of bright square. From in here Sefa can see nothing out there but light.

Under the nearer window an old woman sits at a sloped desk. She's small and straight-backed, in an undyed habit with a faded sunburst stitched at the breast. A roll lies weighted open in front of her, and the last line on it is still wet. She wipes the pen, sets it in its groove, and lines it up. Only then does she lift her head.

A squat iron-bound press stands against the wall beside the desk, shut. On the corner of the desk nearest the door a few crumbs of red wafer lie on the wood, the kind left when someone breaks a letter open with a thumbnail. Nobody has swept them away yet.

The old woman looks at Sefa. First at her face, then at the beads at her wrist, then at her hands, held quiet at her sides. She looks at the hands a moment longer.

"Yes?" she says, and waits.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I keep my hands away from my sword and look at the itemised sheet.

“Master Thole, you sold the forfeit, not a guarantee that nobody would redeem. You’ve confirmed the ticket is valid and we’re here before the term expires.”

I indicate the last line without touching it.

“Show us where Aubrey agreed that redeeming his own pledge would make him liable for your bargain with a later buyer. On the ticket, in the terms posted when he pledged it, or in a contract he signed.”

My voice stays level. “If there’s no such term, strike the sixty. Mistress Vallow has accepted your principal, interest and keeping charge. You receive those in full, and your buyer receives his money back. That’s a redeemed pledge, not a broken promise.”

scenes.narration:
Thole lets Bram finish. He doesn't look at the finger that stops short of his last line. He looks at the ticket under Hesper's fingers, then lowers his spectacles and reads it again from the top, slowly, though he wrote it himself.

Then he opens the ledger at its ribbon and runs his finger down the entry. He doesn't turn the book round this time.

"No," he says. "There is no such term. Not on the ticket, not in my book, not over my door." He pushes the spectacles back up. "Master Vallow agreed to the principal, the house's rate and the keeping. He agreed to nothing else. He couldn't have. The forfeit wasn't sold until this month."

He takes up the pen, draws one line through the sixty, and writes his initials beside it in small letters. Something in the set of his shoulders changes as he does it. It isn't quite relief, but it's close, like a man setting down something he wasn't sure he was allowed to put down.

"What I return to the gentleman is mine to return. That's a matter between him and this house, and it's no affair of yours." He turns the half-sheet round. Under the struck line, in the same small, even hand, he has written *Two hundred and forty.* "But understand the rest of it, Master Halloway, since you're fond of terms. The coffer comes off my shelf when the coin is on my counter. The full sum, in gold, before sundown, from the hand that holds the ticket. Not a promise, not a note of hand. I'll write it in my book as redeemed by the heir, producing the ticket, and I'll give the lady a receipt that says so in those words. Then anyone who asks can read it."

He doesn't say who might ask. His thumb finds the balance pan and rests there.

Hesper reads the new line. She doesn't thank him.

"Two hundred and forty, in gold, before sundown, from my hand." She ties the ticket back into the bundle and knots the tape twice. "I'll fetch it." She lifts her eyes to Thole. "The receipt in those words. Exactly those."

"Exactly those," Thole says.

Hesper turns to Bram with the bundle against her coat. By the door the runner boy has his hands behind his back and his eyes on the struck line. Through the thick green panes the shape on the near end of the bakehouse bench hasn't moved.

"My house, then," Hesper says, low. "And back." She doesn't ask which way. She's waiting for him to choose.

*(Out of game: no roll was needed. Bram's argument was true, and Thole answered it on its merits.)*

 *(Out of game: I didn't roll because what Bram said was true, and at this table true statements aren't rolled. Thole checked his own book, found no such term, and struck the sixty.)*

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa steps just far enough inside to let the door settle, and folds her hands in front of her without making it look like a brag of stillness.

"Your door said ring, ma'am. I hope I've not pulled you off a line you wanted to keep."

Her voice stays low under the vault, pitched the way a woman learns in a sickroom where sound carries too well.

"I'm called Sefa Marrin. I'm here ahead of a widow of this town who needs two things from the rolls. First, to know how a petition to the court of contracts is properly entered—what words, what mark, what proof of her right." A pause. "She'll come up herself and set her hand to it, whatever you tell us. I'm only the one sent to learn the shape of the room before she walks in."

She doesn't move toward the desk yet, and she doesn't take in the room with greed. Her eyes do go to the half-open arched door at the far end, once, and then return to the old woman's face.

"And second, when the petition's in, the moneylender's asked a writing from the court that names her as bearer. He's set the sun as the hour. So we'd be obliged for any mercy of speed the court allows, if the roll comes to it."

She stops there. She does not say the coffer, the seal, or Ashby's name.

"Is it Sister Maudra Kell I'm addressing?"

The old woman hears her out. She doesn't move while Sefa talks, and when Sefa finishes she doesn't answer straight away. She looks down at the roll in front of her, at the wet last line, and lays a strip of blotting paper over it before she says anything.

"I am Maudra Kell." Her voice is level and carries no further than it has to. "You've pulled me off nothing that won't keep."

"Sefa Marrin. Master Halloway gave me your name. He said you might come." She rests two fingers on the edge of the blotting paper. "There is no petition to enter. The widow came herself, by the square door, a little before you rang. She has gone to the Scales with Master Halloway. He asked me to tell you so if you came, and now I have."

"You came in by the nave," Sister Maudra says. "Did you go through the Scales with him this morning?" She doesn't wait for a yes. "Then I'll ask you a thing I didn't ask him, because he wouldn't have known what I meant." She speaks slowly, a word at a time, the way she does everything. "When Thole held his light near that coffer, did the flame stand straight?"

Behind Sefa the heavy door has swung nearly shut. At the far end of the room the half-open arched door lets in a strip of bright square and the faint noise of a cart. Sister Maudra waits at her sloped desk with her two fingers on the paper.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
“May we take the corrected account?” I ask Thole. “We’ll bring it back with the coin.”

At the door, I quietly tell Hesper, “The swordsman followed us from the temple. He’s on the bakehouse bench. We’ll keep to busy streets, and you beside me.”

I check the street before stepping out, then escort her home by the main street and her lane, watching whether the man follows or anyone moves to intercept us. I keep my shield ready and my sword sheathed.

“If he follows us into the lane, we won’t lead him to your gold. We’ll stay where there are people.”

scenes.narration:
"Take it." Thole slides the half-sheet across the counter. The sixty is struck through and his initials sit small beside it. "My book holds the same figures. Bring it back with the coin and I'll write the receipt beneath it, so the two stay together." He lowers his spectacles to the ledger again, as if the two of them had already gone.

The runner boy opens the door for them without being asked.

Bram stops in the doorway, with the green window to one side, and speaks low to Hesper. The swordsman followed them down from the temple and is sitting on the bakehouse bench. They'll keep to busy streets, and she's to walk beside him. Hesper doesn't look across the street. She settles the bundle higher under her arm and says, "Beside you, then."

Bram looks the street over before he steps down. The old man is still asleep at the far end of the bench. The man in road leathers sits at the near end with his elbows on his knees, and he has finished his bread. Carters are going up toward the temple, and a woman is haggling at the chandler's door. Nobody is waiting at either corner.

They walk down the main street at a working pace, with Hesper on the inside, nearest the shop fronts, and Bram's shield between her and the road. He reads the street behind them the same way he did before, in dark shop windows and in where a carter's eyes go. Within a few doors the man on the bench gets up. He comes down the far side of the street, thirty or forty feet back, at the same long, even stride. He doesn't close the gap.

Something else moves before they reach the Red Sheaf. Behind them the latch of the Scales lifts, and the runner boy jumps the hollow step with a folded paper flat against his chest. He trots past them on the far side, past the man in leathers, who doesn't look at him. He turns in under the Sheaf's stable arch and is up the outside stair before Bram draws level with the arch. In the yard the groom is leading the bay mare out. On the mounting block, with his back to the street, a bare-armed boy is talking to someone Bram can't see past the mare's flank. The boy looks round at the sound of the runner's feet on the stair. It's Wat. His eyes go past the runner, out under the arch to the street, and find the grey bonnet walking beside the chain mail. He stops talking.

Bram doesn't stop walking. Hesper doesn't turn her head, but her fingers tighten on the tape round her bundle.

Past the Sheaf the street climbs and bends. The cooper's corner comes into view, and the trough is empty, its water still in the sun. Bram turns Hesper into the lane. Behind them the man in road leathers comes up to the corner and doesn't follow them in. He stops at the trough and sits down on its rim, where Wat sat this morning, with the mouth of the lane in front of him and the main street behind him. He settles himself like a man who expects to wait a while.

The lane is quiet. Hammers ring down by the forges. Hesper has her key out before they reach the door. She lets them in, slides the bolt home behind them, and stands a moment in the brown dimness of the hall with her back to the oak.

"He's at the corner," she says. It isn't a question. "And the stable boy from the trough was in the Sheaf's yard, and he saw me." She takes off her bonnet and hangs it on its peg. "The money is upstairs. It will take me a few minutes." Then she turns back to him with her hand on the newel post.

"Two hundred and forty in gold is a weight a man notices on a woman's arm, Master Halloway. Do we carry it back past him at the front, or out the back, the way we went this morning? He'll be watching the lane. He may not know the alley."

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa doesn't let the stillness break. She meets the old woman's eyes and answers without flourish.

"Yes, Sister. I was there when he lifted his lamp to the grille." Her voice has dropped, almost to the pitch of the room. "The flame didn't stand. It leaned toward the coffer, low and steady, the way grass lies over in a wind that only the grass can feel. It had done the same three days ago, when the widow was there." She pauses, one hand turning the beads at her wrist without looking down. "And the wax was warm that morning, he said. In the first week of the year, with the iron cold under it."

She lets the words settle, then asks, quietly, "Why do you ask it, Sister Maudra? What's written in your rolls about a thing that makes a flame bow?"

scenes.narration:
Sister Maudra doesn't answer straight away. She looks at Sefa's hand turning the beads, then down at the strip of blotting paper on her roll. She lifts it off. She dips the pen and writes one more line under the wet one, slowly, a word at a time. From the door Sefa can see the pen moving but can't read the words. When it's done she wipes the nib and lays the pen in its groove.

"Leaned," she says. "Three days ago, and again today. And the wax was warm in the first week of the year." She looks at the line she has just written. "That is what I needed from someone who stood at the grille. Now it is in the roll."

Then she answers Sefa's question, in the same level voice she uses for everything.

"Two hundred years ago this house made seals to witness oaths between merchant houses. There were four. A sun with a key standing through it. The wax was made here, under the morning light, and light still knows it. That is why your flame bowed." She folds her hands on the desk. "We called them dawn-witness seals. Our rolls list all four as lost in the fire, ninety years ago. I have read that entry more times than I could count. Something that burned ninety years ago has no business being warm on a moneylender's shelf."

She stops there a moment, as if weighing whether the next part is hers to say. She decides it is.

"The roll says one thing more. When such a seal was set, a name was spoken into the wax. It opens for the hand that was named. For any other hand it takes fire and burns whatever it keeps." She says it as plainly as she might give the price of candles. "Master Vallow asked me last autumn how one is opened. I couldn't tell him. I hadn't found the page yet. I found it after he was buried."

Outside the far window a cart goes by on the square, and its wheels rattle and fade. The strip of bright square at the end of the short passage stays empty.

Sister Maudra looks at Sefa's hands again, quiet at her sides now that the beads have stopped.

"When the flame leaned," she says, "did your hands feel it?"

"The back, then." She is already on the stair. "You carry it on the walk. At the counter it comes back to my hand, and I pay him. That's the condition."

Her steps go up and cross the floor overhead. A board creaks, a drawer runs out, and a heavy lid lifts and drops.

Bram goes down the passage to the kitchen. The yard door is shut, but nobody has barred it. The bar leans against the wall where he propped it at half past ten, when they went out the back, and the house has stood open at the rear ever since. He looks round the kitchen. The drainboard is tidy, the hearth is cold and the one cup is still upturned where it was. The bolts and latch are as they were, and nothing seems to have been moved. He sets the bar back in its brackets.

Hesper comes down a few minutes later with a small wooden tray and a sheet of clean paper, and she counts the money out on the kitchen table in front of him. She does it like a clerk, not a widow. She makes four stacks of sixty, checks each one twice with a fingertip, then rolls each stack tight in a strip of paper and folds the ends in. "Two hundred and forty," she says when the last roll is done. The rolls go into a plain canvas meal-sack, the kind any kitchen in Beregost has a dozen of. She twists the neck and ties it off with string. When Bram lifts it, it is heavy for its size and doesn't make a sound.

She looks at the bar in its brackets and then at him.

"It was open the whole time we were out." She says it flatly, the way she'd enter a figure in a column. "We go out by it again. Leave it."

Bram lifts the bar off again. He crosses the yard past the woodpile and stops at the gate to listen. Down below, the forges keep up their steady ringing, and a cart grinds somewhere on the main street. Nothing nearer moves. He lifts the latch and looks through a narrow gap. The coal smoke still lies along the alley at head height. The cat is back on its wall, and it opens one eye at him. No doorways are occupied and no faces are at the windows. The alley is empty from end to end.

He brings her through, and she drops the latch behind them herself.

They take the same way as before, down the smoky side and through the yard behind the two smithies. The apprentices are at the anvils now, and nobody looks up from the work. They come out through the gap between the forge and the stable, and Bram turns them away from the Sheaf's midden smell, one lane further back along the garden path. The woman in the bean rows has moved two rows on. A child runs a hoop along the path toward them, swerves round Bram's legs and away. Hesper walks beside him with her hands empty. She keeps glancing at the sack on his arm and away again. Nobody falls in behind them.

The gap between the wheelwright's and the dyer's lets them out onto the main street, high up toward the temple end. The noon bell hasn't rung yet. It's a few minutes before noon.

Below them the street runs down past the saddler's to the brass scale hanging over Thole's door. Nobody is waiting on the hollow step. Across the way the bakehouse bench has only the old man on it, asleep at the far end. The near end is empty. Further down are the Sheaf's swept step and its stable arch. Past that the street bends out of sight toward the cooper's corner. At this distance the trough is a grey line in the sun, and a single dark shape is sitting on its rim, too far off to be anything more than a shape.

The Scales is a minute's walk down the hill.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa glances down at her own palms as if the question has brought back the sensation. "They prickled," she says. "Not the cold of the strongroom. Like standing too near a lit brazier, the heat searching for a place to enter." She turns her hands over once, slowly, and lets them fall. "I've felt the like before in sickrooms, when fever runs high. But this had a direction to it."

She steps half a pace into the room but doesn't drift toward the desk. "You said a name is spoken into the wax, and it opens for that hand only." She chooses her next words with care. "Would our rolls say anything of how the wax knows the difference? Whether it needs the name said aloud at the hinge, or the hand that belongs to whoever bears the name now? Because if the coffer's been sitting eight months on a shelf while its named hand goes unclaimed, that's one kind of stillness. But if the wax is waiting for a hand that's already in this town..." She lets the sentence hang.

"Aubrey had no widow's mark on it. He carried it to Thole in winter and never told her whose hand it waits for." Her voice is soft, like someone thinking aloud over a difficult remedy. "Could the seal have been made up fresh, Sister? New wax, old device? The moneylender said it was set when the iron was cold, and the flame bowed in his counting-room a ninety-year-old way." She pauses. "You've set the wax on the page just now. You've seen its manners before, maybe. What does it mean if the thing isn't dead?"

scenes.narration:
Sister Maudra watches Sefa turn her hands over. She doesn't write this time. She rests two fingers on the edge of the roll, beside the line she has just added, and waits until Sefa has finished.

"A direction," she says. Then she answers the questions in order.

"How it knows. The page says the one who sets the seal speaks the name into the wax while it is still soft, in morning light. After that the wax knows the hand. It doesn't know the word. Saying the name at the hasp does nothing. Any clerk could say a name." She looks at the roll, not at Sefa. "Whether the hand has to be living, the page doesn't say. It was written for merchant houses, by men who expected to live."

"Fresh wax, old device." She shakes her head once. "Any engraver with a good eye could cut the device again. Nobody could make the wax again. It was made here, at dawn, by the archivists of that day, and the roll gives the amount: enough for four seals and no more. If your flame bowed, it's our wax." She pauses. "The same page says a set seal stays warm for as long as it keeps. That's the word it uses. Keeps."

She lifts her fingers off the paper.

"So it was set within the year, by someone who had wax this house hasn't made in two hundred years. Or it was set before the fire and has stayed warm for ninety years on somebody's shelf. I don't know which. Master Vallow didn't strike me as a man who would have had either." She doesn't make anything more of that.

"What it means if the thing isn't dead." For the first time she answers slowly. "They were made to witness an oath between two houses. A seal that's still warm is still witnessing one. That's all I can tell you, and the roll doesn't tell me either. I'd like to know between whom."

Out on the square a cart goes by and the sound dies away. The strip of light at the end of the short passage stays empty.

Sister Maudra looks at Sefa's hands again, quiet at her sides now.

"I've kept these rolls fifty years," she says. "I've held that page in my own hands and felt nothing from it. Yours knew the wax through iron bars." She doesn't ask her where that comes from. She picks up the pen instead and holds it out over the desk, nib up, toward Sefa.

"The dawnmaster reads what I write this afternoon. What you saw at the grille is already in it. A witness's name under it carries more weight than an archivist's 'I was told'." Her voice stays level. "Will you put yours to it, Sefa Marrin?"

 *(Out of game: Sefa's questions didn't need a roll. She asked them plainly and Maudra answered each one from the page she has read, all in the last turn.)*

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
I walk Hesper straight down to the Scales, keeping her beside me and the sack close. I pull the bell and wait with her at the door, watching the street until we’re admitted.

At the counter, I hand the sack back to her. “Your coin, Mistress Vallow. Two hundred and forty, as counted.”

I lay Thole’s corrected reckoning beside it. “The receipt beneath this, as agreed. And please show us the seal whole before handing the coffer over.”

I stay beside Hesper while she presents the ticket and pays, leaving the transaction in her hands.

scenes.narration:
Bram takes Hesper down the hill at a working pace. She walks on the inside, by the shop fronts, and he keeps the sack tight against his side, under his arm. They pass the saddler's apprentice, still stitching his girth in the doorway. Nobody is waiting on the hollow step under the brass scale.

He pulls the bell. While they wait he looks down the street. The near end of the bakehouse bench is empty and the old man is still asleep at the other. The Red Sheaf's step is swept and the stable arch stands open. Past the bend, the trough is a grey line in the sun with a dark shape on its rim. As Bram watches, the shape stands up. It comes down the far side of the street toward the Sheaf with a long, even stride and turns in under the stable arch without looking up the hill. Bram loses it in the shadow of the yard.

Up behind the roofs the bell of the Song of the Morning starts ringing noon.

The latch lifts and the runner boy lets them in.

---

Thole is at his ledger. He looks up as the bell finishes. Bram sets the sack down on the dark wood in front of Hesper and takes his hand off it. "Your coin, Mistress Vallow. Two hundred and forty, as counted." He lays the corrected reckoning beside it, with the struck sixty and the small initials showing. He asks for the receipt beneath it, as agreed, and for a sight of the seal, whole, before the coffer changes hands.

"As agreed," Thole says.

Hesper unties her bundle first. She takes out the ticket and lays it on the counter, and only after that does she unknot the string on the sack. She takes out the four paper rolls one at a time and sets them in a row. Thole doesn't touch them yet. He looks at the ticket, then at the row, and lowers his spectacles.

He opens the first roll and counts the coins onto the balance pan in a soft, steady patter. Then he weighs them against his brass weights, and does the same with each roll in turn. It takes a while. The pans settle level four times. When the last coins are on the counter he pushes his spectacles up and says, "Two hundred and forty." He doesn't say it to either of them in particular.

"Now the seal," Hesper says.

He takes the key on its cord, lifts the counter flap and picks up the lamp. The grated door opens, and through it Bram sees the counting-room desk with everything squared. The waybill with the carrier's mark has gone from where it lay this morning. Then Thole is at the iron door, the box-lock turns over with a heavy sound, and he comes back carrying the coffer by its two straps, the way he said he always does. He sets it on the counter and puts the lamp down beside it.

The wax is pale and nearly gold, and in the lamplight it looks warm, as it did before. The sun-disc is split by its upright key, and the ring of tiny marks round the rim is clear enough now to see each stroke. Bram can't read any of them. They aren't letters he has seen on any bill or road-stone between here and Amn. Nothing is cracked or lifted, and there's no thumbprint and no smear. The seal is whole.

The lamp flame leans toward the wax across a foot of counter.

Hesper looks at it for a long moment. She doesn't touch the wax. She puts two fingers on the iron beside the hasp, as if she's testing a stove, and takes them away again.

"Whole," she says.

Thole draws the reckoning toward him, dips the pen and writes beneath the struck line. He turns it round for her to read:

Hesper reads the receipt through once more, folds it along its creases and ties it into her bundle with the marriage lines and the will. She doesn't thank him. She does put the empty meal-sack over her arm.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa holds the sister's look for a long moment. Then she steps to the desk with the quiet, particular care of a woman approaching a sickbed, and she takes the pen.

"In my own hand, yes." She dips it and writes her name in the space Sister Maudra shows her, without flourish and without blotting. Before she lets the pen go, she says, low, "Let the record also say that Sefa Marrin came to this house on another's errand and stayed to answer a question about warm wax. That's more than I expected to give today."

She lays the pen down as carefully as the old woman had. "I serve the Lantern. It isn't a temple or a trade, Sister, so I won't dress it up. But light answers light in this place. What I know of the Lantern I'd have called a lamp in a dark ward, once. After the strongroom, I'm not so sure the Lantern doesn't have older kin than the hospice sisters taught." She lets that stand, not a confession, more an offering between two people who keep records.

"One practical thing." She half-turns toward the half-open arched door and the square beyond, but doesn't move toward it. "The widow's gone to Thole with Lord Halloway, you said. Is that by the square door?" She waits for the nod. "Then I'd best move. But if there's a way to set a watch on that coffer between now and sundown—a boy you trust, a brother who passes the Scales like he belongs there—I'd count it a kindness. There's a man in road leathers on your wall outside who has been counting the doors of this building too. He went up from the Red Sheaf with a heel of bread and no prayer in him, and he's still at the square door." She doesn't raise her voice. "I don't know that he means you harm. I know he means to watch something, and that it stands at your small door."

scenes.narration:
Sister Maudra doesn't hand the pen over until Sefa is at the desk. Then she turns the roll a quarter toward her and lays one finger on the bare space below the last line. Sefa has to stand over the entry to sign it, and the words come clear to her the way all writing does, in the same small, upright hand all the way down:

*Mistress Hesper Vallow, widow of Aubrey Vallow, notary, came for the paper he left in my keeping, and it was given to her. She would not say whether the thing he pledged at the Scales bears a seal. Master Bram Halloway, who came with her, has seen it and left the answer to her. Sefa Marrin, who stood at the grille, says the flame leaned toward the wax three days past and again today, and that the wax was warm in the first week of the year. I hold it to be one of ours.*

Sefa signs her name under it with no flourish and doesn't blot it.

Maudra hears out what Sefa wants the record to say. She dips the pen herself and adds a short line beside the name: *witness; came on another's errand.* "That is the part that belongs in a roll," she says. "The rest is yours."

When Sefa speaks of the Lantern, the old woman sets the pen in its groove and lines it up, and she looks at Sefa's face this time, not her hands. She lets a moment pass.

"Older kin." She says it flatly, the way she'd read back a figure. "The page tells me who made the wax, and at what hour, and how much of it. It doesn't tell me whose light the archivists of that day thought they were working by. Nobody thought they needed to write that down." She leaves it there. She doesn't ask what the Lantern is.

Then she answers the practical things in order.

"The square door, yes. It's through there." She tips her head toward the short passage and the strip of bright square. "They left a quarter of an hour before you rang, perhaps a little less."

"A watch." She folds her hands on the desk. "I have no brothers to send, Sefa Marrin. I have rolls. Who goes where for this house is the dawnmaster's to say, and he'll say it when he has read this." She looks down at the entry. "I won't send a boy to stand outside a moneylender's door on my own account. I said I wouldn't take the coffer from the widow's hands, and a watcher of mine on that street would be halfway to doing it."

When Sefa mentions the man in road leathers, the archivist turns her head toward the far window, though she can't see the wall from there and doesn't pretend she can.

"I didn't see him. From this desk I see sky." She picks up the pen again and writes one more line, slowly, under Sefa's name. Sefa can read it as the nib moves: *A man in road leathers sat on the square wall this morning watching the archive door. Not known to me.* Maudra wipes the nib. "Now the dawnmaster will know that too." Then, in the same level voice: "Brother Tam sweeps those steps from the bell until noon, every day. If anyone on the square sat too long, he'll have seen it. He talks to anyone who stops."

She lays the blotting paper over the wet lines, and the entry with Sefa's name in it disappears under the strip.

At the far end of the room the passage runs to the half-open arched door. All the strip of square shows is sun on paving, with nobody crossing it.

<<<
Sister Maudra doesn't hand the pen over until Sefa is at the desk. Then she turns the roll a quarter toward her and lays one finger on the bare space below the last line. Sefa has to stand over the entry to sign it, and the words come clear to her the way all writing does, in the same small, upright hand all the way down:

*Mistress Hesper Vallow, widow of Aubrey Vallow, notary, came for the paper he left in my keeping, and it was given to her. She would not say whether the thing he pledged at the Scales bears a seal. Master Bram Halloway, who came with her, has seen it and left the answer to her. Sefa Marrin, who stood at the grille, says the flame leaned toward the wax three days past and again today, and that the wax was warm in the first week of the year. I hold it to be one of ours.*

Sefa signs her name under it with no flourish and doesn't blot it.

Maudra hears out what Sefa wants the record to say. She dips the pen herself and adds a short line beside the name: *witness; came on another's errand.* "That is the part that belongs in a roll," she says. "The rest is yours."

When Sefa speaks of the Lantern, the old woman sets the pen in its groove and lines it up, and she looks at Sefa's face this time, not her hands. She lets a moment pass.

"Older kin." She says it flatly, the way she'd read back a figure. "The page tells me who made the wax, and at what hour, and how much of it. It doesn't tell me whose light the archivists of that day thought they were working by. Nobody thought they needed to write that down." She leaves it there. She doesn't ask what the Lantern is.

Then she answers the practical things in order.

"The square door, yes. It's through there." She tips her head toward the short passage and the strip of bright square. "They left a quarter of an hour before you rang, perhaps a little less."

"A watch." She folds her hands on the desk. "I have no brothers to send, Sefa Marrin. I have rolls. Who goes where for this house is the dawnmaster's to say, and he'll say it when he has read this." She looks down at the entry. "I won't send a boy to stand outside a moneylender's door on my own account. I said I wouldn't take the coffer from the widow's hands, and a watcher of mine on that street would be halfway to doing it."

When Sefa mentions the man in road leathers, the archivist turns her head toward the far window, though she can't see the wall from there and doesn't pretend she can.

"I didn't see him. From this desk I see sky." She picks up the pen again and writes one more line, slowly, under Sefa's name. Sefa can read it as the nib moves: *A man in road leathers sat on the square wall this morning watching the archive door. Not known to me.* Maudra wipes the nib. "Now the dawnmaster will know that too." Then, in the same level voice: "Brother Tam sweeps those steps from the bell until noon, every day. If anyone on the square sat too long, he'll have seen it. He talks to anyone who stops."

She lays the blotting paper over the wet lines, and the entry with Sefa's name in it disappears under the strip.

At the far end of the room the passage runs to the half-open arched door. All the strip of square shows is sun on paving, with nobody crossing it.

Where you are: on the step outside Hesper Vallow's oak door, Beregost · Time: Day 1 · morning

Sefa steps in past the threshold, the little beads at her wrist clicking once as she moves. She doesn't rush; her hands stay where they can be seen, and her voice is low: "You've got the shutters shut on a fine morning, Mistress Vallow. Something out there you don't like the look of, or something in here you want kept from the sun?" It's said quietly, not needling. Her eyes go around the dim hall rather than to the woman.

Pell slowly and idly turns his head up the lane toward the main street, as if he's only taking in the morning. Then he steps off the step and through the door, saying quietly as he passes her, not unkindly: "Shutters closed and a glance up the street like that. Whoever you're expecting, I'd like to know their face before I'm out there after dark looking for it. Inside's fine for the telling."

You turn your head up the lane, the way you'd look over a stretch of road with too many trees beside it. A step behind you, Pell does the same, slowly and idly, a man taking in the morning.
