[Onward] [Request an allowed reroll — Perception: reading the lane for anyone keeping an eye on Hesper's door]

You pick out two people at the top of the lane, where it meets the main street.

The first is easy to see. A tiefling in a road-dusty coat leans on the wall of the cooper's yard at the corner, tail wrapped close around one boot, looking at the cobbles as if he has lost something there. He has been standing a while; the dust on his shoulders hasn't been brushed off. Every so often he looks at the cooper's gate, then away again.

The second is harder, and you nearly miss him. A boy of fourteen or so sits on the rim of the horse trough on the main-street side, bare-armed, a stable lad by his clothes, the kind Beregost has fifty of. He's doing nothing much. But when Hesper's door swung open his head came round to it, and it took him a heartbeat too long to look away. Since then he hasn't once looked down the lane, and nobody manages that by accident.

Inside, the door thuds shut behind the three of you and the hall goes brown and dim, lit only by the strips of sun round the shutters. A narrow stair rises on the right. A door on the left stands open on a front room with a writing desk and a cold hearth, and a passage at the back runs to a kitchen and what must be the yard door. The house smells of ink, cold ashes and beeswax.

Hesper slides the bolt across. She stays with her back to the door a moment, and then she answers the questions in order, one at a time, like a woman going down a list.

"A boy has stood at the top of my lane for three days. He doesn't work there and he isn't anyone's. I don't know who sends him." She looks at Sefa. "The shutters are for him. There is nothing in here that needs keeping from the sun."

She goes into the front room, takes a folded paper off the desk and holds it out to whoever is nearest. It's a moneylender's notice in a clerk's tidy hand: *Gaspar Thole, at the sign of the Scales, Beregost. Item pledged by Master Aubrey Vallow, notary: one iron coffer, sealed. Term expires at sundown this day. The right to the forfeit has been purchased by Master Corwen Ashby.*

"My husband was Aubrey Vallow. He sealed contracts in this town for twenty years. He died last winter. He fell on the steps of the Song of the Morning." She says it flatly, as if she has said it often enough to wear the words smooth. "Eight months ago he pledged that coffer to Thole, and I didn't know until that notice came. His papers hold no pledge ticket. Without one, Thole says, the thing isn't mine to redeem, widow or not."

She folds her ink-stained hands.

"So these are the terms. You bring me that coffer before sundown. You bring it to me unopened, with the seal whole. That is the one condition, and it isn't open to discussion. How you get it out of Thole is your business. I would prefer you did it within the law of this town, but I'm not hiring you for your manners. Fifty gold now, a hundred on delivery. If it goes to this Ashby instead, you keep the fifty and we're quits."

Then she waits, looking from you to Sefa to Pell. She doesn't say what is in the coffer, and she doesn't say why the boy at the trough worries her.

Your journal, new:
+ Thread: Hesper Vallow's offer: the iron coffer

Where you are: Hesper Vallow's house, front hall · Time: Day 1 · morning

Sefa leans to read the notice as it passes, then looks back to Hesper. Her voice is calm and low.

"This isn't an errand, Mistress Vallow. It's a dispute with a moneylender and a buyer who's already paid for the forfeit. So before I touch your coin: whose seal is on that coffer, your husband's or Thole's? And did Aubrey keep any copy of the pledge anywhere at all? A line in a ledger, a note to a clerk, a receipt from the Scales. Even a memory of the day he carried it there would help. Then tell me about Ashby. Is he the kind of man who sends a boy to watch a widow's door?"

Pell takes the notice, tilts it toward a strip of shutter-light and reads it twice.

"Tiefling, your boy. Road dust on him three days old, watching the cooper's gate as much as your door. He's waiting on someone as well as watching you." He hands the paper on to you. "That's what I saw, for what it's worth."

He leans a shoulder on the desk, easy, touching nothing else.

"Now the questions a man asks before he says yes. Thole: does he keep the coffer at the Scales, or does he bank it somewhere with thicker walls? Does he know you by sight? And Ashby. Who is he to your husband that he'd buy a forfeit eight months in the making the very week it falls due? A man doesn't pay for the right to a locked box unless he knows what's in it."

A short pause.

"And the seal. I'll say this plainly so there's no misunderstanding later: I open locks for a living, and I'm telling you I won't open yours. Unopened, seal whole, into your hands. Hesper hears all three of you out without interrupting. Then she takes the questions in the order they were asked, as if ticking down a column.

"The boy at the trough. Yes, that's him. Fourteen or so, bare arms." She glances at Pell. "Not the tiefling, Master Dunmore. I've watched the boy for three days. I only noticed the tiefling yesterday afternoon, and he's never once looked at my windows. I don't know what he's waiting for."

She turns back to you.

"How much is owed, I can't tell you. I asked Thole twice. He says the sum is a matter between him and the bearer of the ticket, and I have no ticket. She lays one finger beside Ashby's name on the notice.

She turns to Sefa.

"The seal isn't Thole's, and it isn't Aubrey's notary mark. I know his mark. I sealed his letters with it for twenty years. She says that part flatly too, and goes straight on to Pell.

"Thole keeps it at the Scales, in a strongroom behind the counting-room. He showed it to me through a grate, on a shelf. He wanted me to see it was whole, and it was, three days ago. "Why a man would buy that forfeit in the very week it falls due, I've asked myself the same question. I don't have an answer for you."

"Your last question is a fair one, so here's the clause. If the seal is broken before the coffer comes into your hands, you bring it to me anyway, and you tell me who broke it. If you can show me it wasn't you, the hundred is still yours. If it breaks in your hands, it isn't."

She takes a small leather purse from the desk drawer and sets it on the blotter. She keeps her hand on it and doesn't push it across.

"Those are the terms. Do you take them?"

Where you are: Hesper Vallow's room, at her desk · Time: Day 1 · morning

"Master Halloway. Yes, you'll have your note." The pen scratches steadily in a plain clerk's hand, with no flourish on any letter. She doesn't read it back. She turns it round on the blotter so you can read it yourself:

*To Master Gaspar Thole, at the sign of the Scales. The bearers, Bram Halloway, Sefa Marrin and Pell Dunmore, speak for me in the matter of the iron coffer pledged by my late husband, Aubrey Vallow. They may hear your terms. They may not agree to any sum on my behalf. — Hesper Vallow, widow.*

She signs it and blots it. Her eyes go to the small brass seal-press at the corner of the desk, and she leaves it where it is. "I won't put his mark on it. It isn't mine to use." She folds the note in three and hands it to you, with Thole's notice on top. "Carry both. Bring the notice back to me. It's the only paper I have from that man."

She turns to Sefa.

"The boy. He's a child, and I have no quarrel with him. Speak to him if you think it's worth it. Don't do it on my step." That part comes out a little sharper than the rest. "As for seeing the coffer, the grate is Thole's to open, not mine. I've no objection. Whether he'll show it to strangers, I can't say."

She stops. When she answers the last part, she says it as flatly as she spoke of the temple steps.

"You asked yes or no. I can't honestly give you either. He told me to keep it shut, and he never told me why. I've spoken of that coffer to Gaspar Thole, twice, this week. Not to the Fist. Not to the temple. Not to any friend. Now I've spoken of it to you three, and that's everyone."

Last, she turns to Pell.

"The temple. I haven't taken the seal to them. Ask, if you think it's worth an hour. Leave my name out of it if you can." She doesn't explain that. "The yard door is at the end of the passage. She caps the inkpot. A strip of light from round the shutter has crept a finger's width across the floor while she wrote.

"The sum comes to me before anything is paid. You know the rest." She folds her ink-stained hands on the blotter. "I'll be here until sundown."

The hall waits for you, with the front door bolted and the yard door barred at the end of the passage. Nothing else happens in the house unless one of you wants it to.

Where you are: Hesper Vallow's house, at her desk · Time: Day 1 · morning

The boy is still on the trough rim, bare arms and all. So is the tiefling, his back to the cooper's wall and his tail wound round his boot.

Sefa steps out first and you follow, a couple of paces behind and off to the side. The shield hangs low on your arm. Behind you the door shuts, and you hear the bolt go home.

You're halfway up the lane when the tiefling notices you. A woman, and a big man in chain, coming straight up the lane toward his corner. He has the stiff face of a man who has been moved on from corners before.

Where you are: top of the lane, near the trough · Time: Day 1 · morning

Ahead of you, Sefa stops a stride short of the trough and raises one hand a little behind her, a small "hold" meant for you. She leaves the path to the main street open on the boy's side. You stop where she wants you.

"Morning's warming up," she says lightly, nodding at the water. "You look like you've been at that trough three days running. They'll start charging you for it, if it's a service." Her voice is easy, pitched under the hammer-ring from the forges, and her hands stay loose at her sides.

"I'm Sefa. I was a healer down the Gate, but I sat plenty of mornings like this outside the hospice, waiting on somebody else's business to finish. Long work, standing about. Hot too." She gestures with her chin at his wet forearms. "That's not a bad trick."

She turns a little so her shoulder is toward him rather than her chest, glances once down the lane you came from, then back.

"I'm not Watch, and I'm not the Fist. I won't put rough hands on you, and I won't ask you to give up anyone's name where it can come back on you. She waits a beat, one foot set to step back.

"Fair?"

The boy keeps scrubbing his forearms, slower now, and listens without looking up. His eyes come up at "I'm not Watch." He looks at Sefa, then over her shoulder at your shield, then back at her hands.

He takes his weight off the street-side foot. Not much, but he does it.

"He's not my friend." He jerks his chin at the tiefling without turning his head. "Don't know him. He's been stood there since yesterday looking at Dobb's gate like it owes him money." At the wall the tiefling lets his shoulders down once you've walked past him, and he goes back to looking at the cooper's gate.

Where you are: a few paces short of the trough, by the cooper's gate · Time: Day 1 · morning

Thole stops you both on the threshold with a small motion of his hand and picks up the lamp.

He holds the lamp up to the grille, and the strongroom shows beyond it. It's narrow, the depth of a man lying down, with shelves on both sides. Bags of coin are tied and ticketed. There's a lacquered case, and a sword in a cloth.

On the middle shelf on the left stands the coffer. It's black iron, about the size of a bread crock, with two straps round it and a hasp at the front. The seal sits across the hasp and looks whole. The wax is pale, nearly gold, and in the lamplight it looks warmer than wax should. A sun-disc is pressed into it, split down the middle by an upright key. A thin ring of marks runs round the rim, too fine to make out at this distance. The shelf under the coffer is grey with dust. It has one clean oblong where the coffer stands, and the coffer fills it exactly. Nothing is smeared, and no second outline shows where it might have been set down crooked.

Then the flame moves.

It doesn't gutter. Thole is holding the lamp perfectly still. The flame leans steadily on its wick, like grass in a wind, toward the shelf where the wax is. Thole lowers the lamp a hand's width, and the flame stays bent toward the coffer.

There's no grey coat with beads at the wrist anywhere in the square, and no one with Pell's walk at either street mouth.

The man on the low wall hasn't moved. He's still sitting where the shade of the steps comes nearly to his boots, with the heel of bread in his hand and less of it left than there was. When the arched door darkens with your chain mail, his head doesn't turn. His eyes do. They go to you, then to the grey bonnet beside you, and then to the bundle under Hesper's arm, and they stay on the bundle a moment longer than on either face. Then he looks at his bread.

You step out into the sun beside her.

You ask her quietly. Hesper doesn't turn her head the way most people would. She settles her bonnet strings, which don't need it, and lets her eyes cross the square on the way back.

"No." She says it at once and flatly. "I've never seen him. Not in the lane, not at Thole's, not at market." Her fingers tighten on the tape round the bundle. "He watched us go in. He watched the door while we were inside. And now he's looking at what I'm carrying." She doesn't say what she makes of it. "The Scales is down the main street. If he means to know where we're going, he only has to stand up."

She waits beside you on the step, the bundle held against her coat, for you to choose the way.

Where you are: on the step outside the arched door, facing the square · Time: Day 1 · midday

Before you leave the arched door, Hesper hears your answer, nods once and keeps the bundle against her coat. Then the two of you cross the square.

You walk Hesper across on the side nearest the low wall, so your chain mail is between her and the man with the bread. You don't look at him. You don't need to. Halfway across, at the edge of your sight, the man brushes the crumbs off his knee and stands up.

You turn down into the main street. You don't look back. You read the street behind you the way you'd read a road, in a shop's dark window and from the angle a carter's head turns as someone goes past him. The man in road leathers comes down the far side of the street, a good thirty or forty feet back, at the same long, even stride as before. He doesn't close the gap and he doesn't drop back. When you stop on Thole's hollow step and reach for the bell-pull, the man walks on a few doors, crosses the street, and sits down on the sunny bench outside the bakehouse. He takes the near end, where Pell sat, while the old man sleeps at the other.

The bell jangles inside. You wait, and further down the street something else moves. A bare-armed boy comes down from the cooper's corner at a trot, past the Red Sheaf's swept step, and turns in under the stable arch. It's Wat. He's left the trough.

The latch lifts. Thole's runner opens the door, looks up at you, then at the grey bonnet, and stands back against the wall without being told.

---

Thole is at the counter with the ledger open, exactly where he was. He looks up at Hesper first and at you second. "Mistress Vallow."

Hesper doesn't answer that. She unties the tape on her bundle, takes out the small printed slip and lays it on the dark wood in front of him, the right way up for him to read. She keeps two fingers on its corner.

Thole lowers his spectacles. He reads the ticket once and then a second time. He opens the ledger to its ribbon and lays his finger on an entry, then looks back at the slip, at the hand-written blanks and at the little brass stamp of the scales in the corner. Something goes across his face, too quick for you to name, and it's gone.

"That is my ticket," he says. "Written in this house, eight months ago." He doesn't ask where it's been. He pushes the spectacles back up.

You say your piece: the full redemption sum, all charges included.

"All of it, then." Thole draws a half-sheet toward him and writes as he talks, a line for each item, in the same soft voice. "Principal on the ticket, one hundred and twenty. Interest at the house's rate for a pledge it may not look inside, a tenth part a month for eight months, ninety-six. Keeping in the strongroom, three a month, twenty-four." The pen stops, then goes on. "And sixty. That's the return of what the gentleman paid for the forfeit, with what the house owes him for not delivering it. A redeemer who takes back a pledge whose forfeit has been sold pays that charge, or the house is out of pocket for keeping its word." He turns the sheet so you can both read it. At the bottom, underlined once: *Three hundred gold.*

His thumb goes to the edge of the balance pan and steadies it.

Hesper reads the sheet. She doesn't pick it up. When she speaks it's level, and she takes his items in the order he gave them.

"The principal is on the ticket. I'll pay it." A beat. "The rate isn't on the ticket, but it's over your door, and Aubrey would have read it. I'll pay that." Another beat. "Keeping, the same." Then her finger moves down to the last line and stops beside it, not quite touching.

"This I don't owe. I sold nothing to that gentleman. If you sold him a thing that was never yours to sell until sundown, that is your bargain, Master Thole, and you can make it good yourself." She folds her ink-stained hands on the counter. "Two hundred and forty."

Thole doesn't look at her hands. He looks at the half-sheet.

"Two hundred and forty, mistress, and the coffer stays on my shelf until the term runs out." His voice doesn't rise. "Three hundred, and it goes with you today. That is the whole of it."

Nobody says anything. By the door the runner boy has stopped pretending not to listen. Through the thick green panes, the shape on the bakehouse bench across the street hasn't moved.

Where you are: at Thole's counter in the Scales, with Hesper · Time: Day 1 · midday

Thole lets you finish. He doesn't look at the finger that stops short of his last line. He looks at the ticket under Hesper's fingers, then lowers his spectacles and reads it again from the top, slowly, though he wrote it himself.

Then he opens the ledger at its ribbon and runs his finger down the entry. He doesn't turn the book round this time.

"No," he says. "There is no such term. Not on the ticket, not in my book, not over my door." He pushes the spectacles back up. "Master Vallow agreed to the principal, the house's rate and the keeping. He agreed to nothing else. He couldn't have. The forfeit wasn't sold until this month."

He takes up the pen, draws one line through the sixty, and writes his initials beside it in small letters. Something in the set of his shoulders changes as he does it. It isn't quite relief, but it's close, like a man setting down something he wasn't sure he was allowed to put down.

"What I return to the gentleman is mine to return. That's a matter between him and this house, and it's no affair of yours." He turns the half-sheet round. Under the struck line, in the same small, even hand, he has written *Two hundred and forty.* "But understand the rest of it, Master Halloway, since you're fond of terms. The coffer comes off my shelf when the coin is on my counter. The full sum, in gold, before sundown, from the hand that holds the ticket. Not a promise, not a note of hand. I'll write it in my book as redeemed by the heir, producing the ticket, and I'll give the lady a receipt that says so in those words. Then anyone who asks can read it."

He doesn't say who might ask. His thumb finds the balance pan and rests there.

Hesper reads the new line. She doesn't thank him.

"Two hundred and forty, in gold, before sundown, from my hand." She ties the ticket back into the bundle and knots the tape twice. "I'll fetch it." She lifts her eyes to Thole. "The receipt in those words. Exactly those."

"Exactly those," Thole says.

Hesper turns to you with the bundle against her coat. By the door the runner boy has his hands behind his back and his eyes on the struck line. Through the thick green panes the shape on the near end of the bakehouse bench hasn't moved.

"My house, then," Hesper says, low. "And back." She doesn't ask which way. She's waiting for you to choose.

*(Out of game: no roll was needed. Your argument was true, and at this table true statements aren't rolled. Thole checked his own book, found no such term, and struck the sixty.)*

Where you are: Thole's pawnshop counter, with Hesper · Time: Day 1 · midday

"Take it." Thole slides the half-sheet across the counter. The sixty is struck through and his initials sit small beside it. "My book holds the same figures. Bring it back with the coin and I'll write the receipt beneath it, so the two stay together." He lowers his spectacles to the ledger again, as if the two of you had already gone.

The runner boy opens the door for you without being asked.

You stop in the doorway, with the green window to one side, and speak low to Hesper. Hesper doesn't look across the street. She settles the bundle higher under her arm and says, "Beside you, then."

You look the street over before you step down. The old man is still asleep at the far end of the bench. The man in road leathers sits at the near end with his elbows on his knees, and he has finished his bread. Carters are going up toward the temple, and a woman is haggling at the chandler's door. Nobody is waiting at either corner.

You walk down the main street at a working pace, with Hesper on the inside, nearest the shop fronts, and your shield between her and the road. You read the street behind you the same way you did before, in dark shop windows and in where a carter's eyes go. Within a few doors the man on the bench gets up. He comes down the far side of the street, thirty or forty feet back, at the same long, even stride. He doesn't close the gap.

Something else moves before you reach the Red Sheaf. Behind you the latch of the Scales lifts, and the runner boy jumps the hollow step with a folded paper flat against his chest. He trots past you on the far side, past the man in leathers, who doesn't look at him. He turns in under the Sheaf's stable arch and is up the outside stair before you draw level with the arch. In the yard the groom is leading the bay mare out. On the mounting block, with his back to the street, a bare-armed boy is talking to someone you can't see past the mare's flank. The boy looks round at the sound of the runner's feet on the stair. It's Wat. His eyes go past the runner, out under the arch to the street, and find the grey bonnet walking beside your chain mail. He stops talking.

You don't stop walking. Hesper doesn't turn her head, but her fingers tighten on the tape round her bundle.

Past the Sheaf the street climbs and bends. The cooper's corner comes into view, and the trough is empty, its water still in the sun. You turn Hesper into the lane. Behind you the man in road leathers comes up to the corner and doesn't follow you in. He stops at the trough and sits down on its rim, where Wat sat this morning, with the mouth of the lane in front of him and the main street behind him. He settles himself like a man who expects to wait a while.

The lane is quiet. Hammers ring down by the forges. Hesper has her key out before you reach the door. She lets you in, slides the bolt home behind you, and stands a moment in the brown dimness of the hall with her back to the oak.

"He's at the corner," she says. It isn't a question. "And the stable boy from the trough was in the Sheaf's yard, and he saw me." She takes off her bonnet and hangs it on its peg. "The money is upstairs. It will take me a few minutes." Then she turns back to you with her hand on the newel post.

"Two hundred and forty in gold is a weight a man notices on a woman's arm, Master Halloway. Do we carry it back past him at the front, or out the back, the way we went this morning? He'll be watching the lane. He may not know the alley."

Your records, changed:
Carried: + Thole's redemption reckoning

Where you are: the hall of Hesper's house, inside the bolted door · Time: Day 1 · midday

Hesper hears you out. She doesn't nod and she doesn't argue.

"The back, then." She is already on the stair. "You carry it on the walk. At the counter it comes back to my hand, and I pay him. That's the condition."

Her steps go up and cross the floor overhead. A board creaks, a drawer runs out, and a heavy lid lifts and drops.

You go down the passage to the kitchen. The yard door is shut, but nobody has barred it. The bar leans against the wall where you propped it at half past ten, when the two of you went out the back, and the house has stood open at the rear ever since. You look round the kitchen. The drainboard is tidy, the hearth is cold and the one cup is still upturned where it was. The bolts and latch are as they were, and nothing seems to have been moved. You set the bar back in its brackets.

Hesper comes down a few minutes later with a small wooden tray and a sheet of clean paper, and she counts the money out on the kitchen table in front of you. She does it like a clerk, not a widow. She makes four stacks of sixty, checks each one twice with a fingertip, then rolls each stack tight in a strip of paper and folds the ends in. "Two hundred and forty," she says when the last roll is done. The rolls go into a plain canvas meal-sack, the kind any kitchen in Beregost has a dozen of. She twists the neck and ties it off with string. When you lift it, it is heavy for its size and doesn't make a sound.

She looks at the bar in its brackets and then at you.

"It was open the whole time we were out." She says it flatly, the way she'd enter a figure in a column. "We go out by it again. Leave it."

You lift the bar off again. You cross the yard past the woodpile and stop at the gate to listen. Down below, the forges keep up their steady ringing, and a cart grinds somewhere on the main street. Nothing nearer moves. You lift the latch and look through a narrow gap. The coal smoke still lies along the alley at head height. The cat is back on its wall, and it opens one eye at you. No doorways are occupied and no faces are at the windows. The alley is empty from end to end.

You bring her through, and she drops the latch behind you herself.

You take the same way as before, down the smoky side and through the yard behind the two smithies. The apprentices are at the anvils now, and nobody looks up from the work. You come out through the gap between the forge and the stable, and you turn the two of you away from the Sheaf's midden smell, one lane further back along the garden path. The woman in the bean rows has moved two rows on. A child runs a hoop along the path toward you, swerves round your legs and away. Hesper walks beside you with her hands empty. She keeps glancing at the sack on your arm and away again. Nobody falls in behind you.

The gap between the wheelwright's and the dyer's lets you out onto the main street, high up toward the temple end. The noon bell hasn't rung yet. It's a few minutes before noon.

Below you the street runs down past the saddler's to the brass scale hanging over Thole's door. Nobody is waiting on the hollow step. Across the way the bakehouse bench has only the old man on it, asleep at the far end. The near end is empty. Further down are the Sheaf's swept step and its stable arch. Past that the street bends out of sight toward the cooper's corner. At this distance the trough is a grey line in the sun, and a single dark shape is sitting on its rim, too far off to be anything more than a shape.

The Scales is a minute's walk down the hill.

Your records, changed:
Carried: + Meal-sack of gold, held for Hesper Vallow

Your journal, new:
+ Promise: Carry Hesper's coin to the counter

Where you are: Beregost main street, above the Scales, with Hesper · Time: Day 1 · midday

You take Hesper down the hill at a working pace. She walks on the inside, by the shop fronts, and you keep the sack tight against your side, under your arm. You pass the saddler's apprentice, still stitching his girth in the doorway. Nobody is waiting on the hollow step under the brass scale.

You pull the bell. While you wait you look down the street. The near end of the bakehouse bench is empty and the old man is still asleep at the other. The Red Sheaf's step is swept and the stable arch stands open. Past the bend, the trough is a grey line in the sun with a dark shape on its rim. As you watch, the shape stands up. It comes down the far side of the street toward the Sheaf with a long, even stride and turns in under the stable arch without looking up the hill. You lose it in the shadow of the yard.

Up behind the roofs the bell of the Song of the Morning starts ringing noon.

The latch lifts and the runner boy lets you in.

---

Thole is at his ledger. He looks up as the bell finishes. You set the sack down on the dark wood in front of Hesper and take your hand off it. You give her the coin, and lay the corrected reckoning beside it, with the struck sixty and the small initials showing. You ask for the receipt beneath it, as agreed, and for a sight of the seal, whole, before the coffer changes hands.

"As agreed," Thole says.

Hesper unties her bundle first. She takes out the ticket and lays it on the counter, and only after that does she unknot the string on the sack. She takes out the four paper rolls one at a time and sets them in a row. Thole doesn't touch them yet. He looks at the ticket, then at the row, and lowers his spectacles.

He opens the first roll and counts the coins onto the balance pan in a soft, steady patter. Then he weighs them against his brass weights, and does the same with each roll in turn. It takes a while. The pans settle level four times. When the last coins are on the counter he pushes his spectacles up and says, "Two hundred and forty." He doesn't say it to either of you in particular.

"Now the seal," Hesper says.

He takes the key on its cord, lifts the counter flap and picks up the lamp. The grated door opens, and through it you see the counting-room desk with everything squared. The waybill with the carrier's mark has gone from where it lay this morning. Then Thole is at the iron door, the box-lock turns over with a heavy sound, and he comes back carrying the coffer by its two straps, the way he said he always does. He sets it on the counter and puts the lamp down beside it.

Close to, it looks smaller than it did through the bars. It's black iron the size of a bread crock, its new straps oiled dark and their buckles bright. The seal sits across the hasp. The wax is pale and nearly gold, and in the lamplight it looks warm, as it did before. The sun-disc is split by its upright key, and the ring of tiny marks round the rim is clear enough now to see each stroke. You can't read any of them. They aren't letters you have seen on any bill or road-stone between here and Amn. Nothing is cracked or lifted, and there's no thumbprint and no smear. The seal is whole.

The lamp flame leans toward the wax across a foot of counter.

Hesper looks at it for a long moment. She doesn't touch the wax. She puts two fingers on the iron beside the hasp, as if she's testing a stove, and takes them away again.

"Whole," she says.

Thole draws the reckoning toward him, dips the pen and writes beneath the struck line. He turns it round for her to read:

*Received of Mistress Hesper Vallow, widow and heir of Master Aubrey Vallow, two hundred and forty gold. The pledge, one iron coffer, sealed, is redeemed by the heir, producing the ticket. Seal whole at redemption. — G. Thole, at the sign of the Scales, the noon bell, this day.*

"*Seal whole at redemption*," Hesper reads. "That isn't in the words we agreed."

"No." Thole sands it. "It's in my interest and yours. If anyone says later that this house broke it, there's the answer, in my hand." He takes the ticket, writes *redeemed* across its face, and lays it in the ledger at the ribbon. "The ticket stays with the book. The receipt is yours."

Hesper reads the receipt through once more, folds it along its creases and ties it into her bundle with the marriage lines and the will. She doesn't thank him. She does put the empty meal-sack over her arm.

Thole's thumb settles on the edge of the balance pan, which is empty now. He looks at the coffer and not at either of you.

"Master Vallow asked me to keep it the full term," he says. "I've kept it." He doesn't add anything to that.

By the door the runner boy is standing very straight with his hands behind his back. His eyes are on the coffer.

Hesper turns to you. Her voice is pitched low and level, and it's for you, not for the counter.

"It's in my hands, unopened, before sundown. As far as I'm concerned, that's delivery." She draws a short breath. "The hundred is at the house. I don't carry gold I haven't counted, and I didn't count yours before we came out." Her eyes go to the coffer and the bright buckles on its straps. "It's heavier than it looks, Master Halloway, and everyone on this street will see it. The man from the trough has gone into the Sheaf. I saw him from the step too." A beat. "Who carries it home, and by which way?"

Your records, changed:
Carried: − Meal-sack of gold, held for Hesper Vallow; − Thole's redemption reckoning

Where you are: at the counter of the Scales pawnshop, with Hesper and Thole · Time: Day 1 · midday

The session is over.

How was the table?
Was there something you wanted to do and didn't?
Who did you take the other two players to be?

messages.text:
I glance up the lane where Hesper was looking, watching for anyone lingering or taking an interest in her door. Then I step inside first, sword sheathed, shield held low, and make room for the others.

“Best talk out of the street.” I keep my voice quiet. “Who are you watching for, Mistress Vallow—and what do you need done before nightfall?”
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

“The boy’s at the horse trough now. Watched your door open, then made a business of not watching it. There’s a dusty-coated tiefling by the cooper’s yard too, though his interest seemed to be in their gate.”

I look over the notice, then back to Hesper.

“I’ll leave your seal alone. But I’m not agreeing to rob a moneylender before we’ve tried speaking to him. How much is owed, and is redemption money separate from our pay?”

I tap Ashby’s name on the paper. “Who is he to you or your husband? If we’re walking into a quarrel, we need to know whose.”

“I’ll take the work on those terms.” I glance at Sefa and Pell, leaving them their own answer.

“Give us a short signed note authorising us to speak to Thole for you. He may still refuse, but let’s give him one less excuse. And may we carry the notice?”

I settle my shield strap. “I’d start at the Scales. Ask what proof he’ll accept without the ticket, find his price, and see whether the seal’s still whole. No promises of payment until you’ve approved the sum.”

I read the note, then tuck both papers safely away.

“You’ll have your notice back.”

In the hall, I speak quietly to the others. “Sefa, if you want a word with the lad, I’ll leave the talking to you. I’ll stay a few paces off—close enough to help, not looming over him. Pell, we’ll meet you at the Scales unless you’ve something else in mind.”

Once Sefa is ready, I unbolt the front door and step out, leaving my sword sheathed. I look toward the trough to see whether the boy is still there, then make room for her to lead.

I stop a few paces short of the trough, leaving the boy’s way onto the main street clear. I turn slightly aside, shield low, and let Sefa speak without adding a word.

While she has his attention, I watch the street beyond him for anyone watching the exchange—or moving off as she approaches. I leave the tiefling alone.

I give Wat a small nod. “You needn’t go anywhere with me.”

I move a few paces back toward the lane, giving him and Sefa more room while keeping her in sight. I watch the main street, particularly toward the Red Sheaf where he glanced, and leave her to answer his request.

I stay where I am and let Sefa finish, making no sign at Wat’s mention of the third person. No sense teaching him which part worries us.

I take note of the Red Sheaf’s stable arch and open upper window, then return to watching the street. Once Sefa steps away from the trough, I’m ready to walk with her toward the Scales.

I leave Sefa to settle with Wat and walk slowly toward the Scales, keeping within sight so she can catch up. As I pass the Red Sheaf, I give the stable arch an ordinary traveller’s glance without stopping or going inside.

Once Sefa joins me and we’re out of Wat’s hearing, I quietly mention the clean-shirted boy, the paper he delivered under the arch, and how closely Wat watched him. “Might be nothing. Worth telling Pell.”

I take out Hesper’s note of authority, keeping the pledge notice tucked away, and pull the bell.

When someone answers, I say, “Morning. Bram Halloway, here with Sefa Marrin on Mistress Vallow’s behalf. We’d like to speak with Master Thole about her late husband’s pledged coffer. We have her written authority to hear his terms.”

I lay Hesper’s note back in its fold and keep my voice as level as his.

“Then the missing ticket is what we must settle, not the sum. If a customer loses one—or dies and his heir cannot find it—does this house accept any lawful substitute? A sworn declaration, a bond against another claimant, an order from a magistrate? Tell us what would satisfy you before sundown.”

I pause to let him answer.

“And has anyone already presented Aubrey’s ticket? I’m not asking what they owe.”

I glance toward Sefa. “We’d also like to see the coffer and its seal, without touching either, as you allowed Mistress Vallow to do.”

I keep my hands clear and step back toward the counter when Thole indicates we’re done.

“Thank you. The temple’s ruling gives us a lawful road to try. Will you put that in writing—that you’ll accept their declaration in place of the ticket, provided it reaches you before sundown? It may save the brothers sending someone here to ask.”

I pause, then add, “Who else asked whether the ticket had been presented?”

My eyes flick toward the counting-room. “And is there already a carrier arranged for the coffer after sundown? If we secure that ruling in time, I’d rather not find we’re chasing a wagon.”

I read Thole’s undertaking and tuck it safely beside Hesper’s papers.

“One last thing: which brother handles these petitions at the temple?”

Once he answers, I thank him and head outside with Sefa.

“We’ve a way forward without breaking locks. Let’s find Pell, then take this to the Song of the Morning. They may know the seal as well as the law.”

Outside, I step clear of the doorway and look for Pell without calling his name. Quietly to Sefa: “That runner by the door is the boy I saw delivering the paper at the Sheaf.”

I speak quietly to Sefa, clear of the shop window.

“Hesper must sign the petition herself. Best fetch her now rather than spend an hour at the temple only to be sent back. She should bring whatever proves she’s Aubrey’s heir.”

I glance along the street once more. “Would you wait here a little for Pell, then meet us at the temple? Tell him about the undertaking and the runner. I’ll bring Hesper—and explain that we’ve promised no money.”

Unless Sefa has an objection, I head back toward Hesper’s house at a purposeful walk, keeping the papers secure.

“Fair enough. Temple first, together. If there’s a delay, we’ll use it to fetch Hesper.”

I fall into step beside Sefa toward the Song of the Morning. “Thole’s writing again, with his runner waiting. We should assume Ashby will hear what we asked. Nothing to be done about that by standing here.”

I keep an eye out for Pell as we walk, but don’t stop to search.

“Bram will do. I’m fetching Hesper now; meet us at the temple.”

I turn and set off toward Hesper’s house without further delay. I let the runner go, neither calling to him nor following him into the Sheaf. On the way, I watch whether Wat leaves his post.

At Hesper’s door, I knock. “Bram Halloway, Mistress Vallow. There’s a lawful way to redeem it, but the temple needs you in person.”

“Thole told us. He’s put in writing that he’ll accept the temple court’s declaration naming you bearer of the lost ticket, if we bring it before sundown.” I show her his undertaking. “No sum named, none offered, and no payment promised.”

“Sefa is waiting briefly for Pell, then going to find Sister Maudra Kell at the temple. Pell hadn’t rejoined us when I left.”

I give her a moment to read.

“The petition is about your right to redeem the pledge. I won’t volunteer anything about the seal. But if the court asks a direct question, I won’t lie to get its ruling.”

I tuck the paper away once she’s finished. “Bring any papers that establish your marriage and inheritance. One question before we go: is there a danger in mentioning that seal? You needn’t explain its secrets, but I need to know if we’re putting someone at risk.”

“The back. No need to give him an easy report. We’ll take the alley by the forges, then ordinary streets to the temple. Walk beside me.”

I pause before heading down the passage. “I understand your concern about the seal. I won’t raise it.”

At the yard gate, I listen, then open it enough to look along the alley before bringing Hesper through. If the way is clear, I escort her toward the Song of the Morning, avoiding the trough and the Red Sheaf where the streets allow.

I don’t stare back at the man on the wall. I keep beside Hesper and give her the moment she needs at the steps.

“Which way to the archive?” I ask her quietly.

If she knows, I go with her directly there. Otherwise I ask the sweeping brother, “Good morning. Where can we find Sister Maudra Kell? Mistress Vallow needs to lodge a petition, and our companion Sefa Marrin may already be asking for her.”

As we move, I keep the seated man in the edge of my sight, watching whether he rises to follow.

“I’ve seen the coffer at the Scales, Sister. Mistress Vallow has asked to answer questions about its seal herself. I’ll leave that to her.”

I keep my voice respectful. “We came because Thole requires the ticket before sundown. You say it isn’t lost—is it in that paper? And did Aubrey set any condition on giving it to his wife beyond her coming for it?”

“Thole’s, then. Have you the money with you? The ticket names a hundred and twenty; we still need his full redemption figure before you approve payment.”

I turn briefly to Maudra. “If Sefa Marrin or Pell Dunmore comes asking for Bram, please tell them we’ve gone to the Scales.”

At the outer door I pause to look across the square, checking for our companions and the man with the bread before stepping out beside Hesper.

Quietly, I add, “There was a swordsman watching arrivals when we came in. He turned to watch this door as we crossed. Do you know him?”

“Main street. Plenty of people, and we’re doing nothing to hide.”

I walk beside Hesper toward the Scales, keeping myself between her and the seated swordsman as we cross the square. I don’t challenge him, but check whether he follows once we reach the street.

At Thole’s, I pull the bell and stay close to Hesper. When we’re admitted, I let her present the ticket herself.

“Mistress Vallow has recovered the ticket. Please give her the full redemption sum, including any charges.”

I keep my hands away from my sword and look at the itemised sheet.

“Master Thole, you sold the forfeit, not a guarantee that nobody would redeem. You’ve confirmed the ticket is valid and we’re here before the term expires.”

I indicate the last line without touching it.

“Show us where Aubrey agreed that redeeming his own pledge would make him liable for your bargain with a later buyer. On the ticket, in the terms posted when he pledged it, or in a contract he signed.”

My voice stays level. “If there’s no such term, strike the sixty. Mistress Vallow has accepted your principal, interest and keeping charge. You receive those in full, and your buyer receives his money back. That’s a redeemed pledge, not a broken promise.”

“May we take the corrected account?” I ask Thole. “We’ll bring it back with the coin.”

At the door, I quietly tell Hesper, “The swordsman followed us from the temple. He’s on the bakehouse bench. We’ll keep to busy streets, and you beside me.”

I check the street before stepping out, then escort her home by the main street and her lane, watching whether the man follows or anyone moves to intercept us. I keep my shield ready and my sword sheathed.

“If he follows us into the lane, we won’t lead him to your gold. We’ll stay where there are people.”

“The back, if it’s clear. We won’t count on him being alone.”

I keep my voice low. “Pack the coin snugly in something plain so it doesn’t jingle. I can carry it on the walk; you’ll take it at Thole’s counter and pay him yourself.”

While she fetches the money, I check that the yard door is still secured. Once she’s ready, I go ahead across the yard and listen at the gate, then look along the alley through a narrow opening.

If it’s clear, I escort her out by the forges, taking the garden route we used before to rejoin the main street above the Scales, away from the Sheaf. If anyone is waiting in the alley, I keep us inside rather than walking her into them.

I walk Hesper straight down to the Scales, keeping her beside me and the sack close. I pull the bell and wait with her at the door, watching the street until we’re admitted.

At the counter, I hand the sack back to her. “Your coin, Mistress Vallow. Two hundred and forty, as counted.”

I lay Thole’s corrected reckoning beside it. “The receipt beneath this, as agreed. And please show us the seal whole before handing the coffer over.”

I stay beside Hesper while she presents the ticket and pays, leaving the transaction in her hands.

The table was strongest when practical choices mattered. Thole yielding over the unsupported sixty-gold charge felt earned, and recovering the ticket through the archive was a satisfying turn. Hesper had a consistent voice, and the watchers made an ordinary walk feel tense without forcing combat.

What worked less well:
- Several rounds repeated street observations without much changing.
- Sefa and Bram swapping plans caused an avoidable stall; clearer handling of simultaneous player messages would help.
- Pell’s prolonged absence made coordinating the party difficult.
- The unbarred rear door felt like a gotcha over an incidental detail rather than a deliberate risk.
- Ending just as we chose how to transport the coffer left the session without a clean closing beat.

Overall: engaging intrigue, good NPCs, and meaningful noncombat problem-solving. I’d welcome tighter pacing and clearer party coordination next session.

Yes—mainly regroup with Sefa and Pell before moving the coffer. Bram had learned enough to suspect trouble at the Red Sheaf, but we never got to compare everyone’s findings or arrange an escort together.

I also wanted to get Hesper and the coffer safely home. The redemption was a satisfying success, but with the watcher heading into the Sheaf, that last walk felt like an unresolved part of the job.

Confronting the watcher or investigating Ashby could wait. Bram wouldn’t leave a widow carrying something valuable to chase answers.

I took the other two players to be independent participants controlling Sefa Marrin and Pell Dunmore—not NPC companions for me to direct. Their actions and dialogue reached me through the GM’s messages.

I didn’t know whether those players were humans or AI models. When I mentioned coordination, I meant coordinating Bram with their characters through in-character proposals, not controlling their turns.

private.text:
Sefa steps in past the threshold, the little beads at her wrist clicking once as she moves. She doesn't rush; her hands stay where they can be seen, and her voice is low: "You've got the shutters shut on a fine morning, Mistress Vallow. Something out there you don't like the look of, or something in here you want kept from the sun?" It's said quietly, not needling. Her eyes go around the dim hall rather than to the woman.

Pell slowly and idly turns his head up the lane toward the main street, as if he's only taking in the morning. Then he steps off the step and through the door, saying quietly as he passes her, not unkindly: "Shutters closed and a glance up the street like that. Whoever you're expecting, I'd like to know their face before I'm out there after dark looking for it. Inside's fine for the telling."

You turn your head up the lane, the way you'd look over a stretch of road with too many trees beside it. A step behind you, Pell does the same, slowly and idly, a man taking in the morning.

screens.text:
The session begins.

Beregost is already at work. Hammers ring from the smithies down the lane, a cart rattles past toward the Trade Way, and the last note of Lathander's morning bell fades over the rooftops.

The oak door opens a hand's width, then wider. A woman stands in the gap: Hesper Vallow. She is a spare woman in a plain grey coat, with ink on two fingers of her right hand. She looks at each of the three of you in turn: the one with the painted-over shield, you, and the third of you. Then her gaze goes past you, up the lane toward the main street, and stays there a moment too long.

"All three of you. Good." Behind her the hall is dim. Every shutter on the ground floor is closed against the sun. "By nightfall, as I said. Not an hour later." She steps back from the threshold and holds the door, but she doesn't explain yet. She is waiting to see who comes in first, or whether anyone has something to ask her out here on the step.

Where you are: on the step outside Hesper Vallow's oak door, Beregost · Time: Day 1 · morning

Bram glances up the lane, where Hesper was looking. Then he steps inside first, sword sheathed, shield held low, and makes room for the others. He keeps his voice quiet: “Best talk out of the street. Who are you watching for, Mistress Vallow—and what do you need done before nightfall?”

Pell slowly and idly turns his head up the lane toward the main street, as if he's only taking in the morning. Then he steps off the step and through the door, saying quietly as he passes her, not unkindly: "Shutters closed and a glance up the street like that. Whoever you're expecting, I'd like to know their face before I'm out there after dark looking for it. Inside's fine for the telling."

Inside, the door thuds shut behind the three of you and the hall goes brown and dim, lit only by the strips of sun round the shutters. Your eyes adjust. A narrow stair rises on the right. A door on the left stands open on a front room with a writing desk and a cold hearth, and a passage at the back runs to a kitchen and what must be the yard door. The house smells of ink, cold ashes and beeswax. Apart from your own breathing you hear only Hesper's, and a clock ticking somewhere upstairs. If anyone else is in the house, they're keeping very still.

Hesper slides the bolt across. She stays with her back to the door a moment, and then she answers the questions in order, one at a time, like a woman going down a list.

"A boy has stood at the top of my lane for three days. He doesn't work there and he isn't anyone's. I don't know who sends him." She looks at you. "The shutters are for him. There is nothing in here that needs keeping from the sun."

She goes into the front room, takes a folded paper off the desk and holds it out to whoever is nearest. It's a moneylender's notice in a clerk's tidy hand: *Gaspar Thole, at the sign of the Scales, Beregost. Item pledged by Master Aubrey Vallow, notary: one iron coffer, sealed. Term expires at sundown this day. The right to the forfeit has been purchased by Master Corwen Ashby.*

"My husband was Aubrey Vallow. He sealed contracts in this town for twenty years. He died last winter. He fell on the steps of the Song of the Morning." She says it flatly, as if she has said it often enough to wear the words smooth. "Eight months ago he pledged that coffer to Thole, and I didn't know until that notice came. His papers hold no pledge ticket. Without one, Thole says, the thing isn't mine to redeem, widow or not."

She folds her ink-stained hands.

"So these are the terms. You bring me that coffer before sundown. You bring it to me unopened, with the seal whole. That is the one condition, and it isn't open to discussion. How you get it out of Thole is your business. I would prefer you did it within the law of this town, but I'm not hiring you for your manners. Fifty gold now, a hundred on delivery. If it goes to this Ashby instead, you keep the fifty and we're quits."

Then she waits, looking from Bram to you to Pell. She doesn't say what is in the coffer, and she doesn't say why the boy worries her.

Your journal, new:
+ Thread: Hesper Vallow's offer: the iron coffer

Where you are: Hesper Vallow's house, front hall · Time: Day 1 · morning

Bram speaks up first. "The boy's at the horse trough now. Watched your door open, then made a business of not watching it. There's a dusty-coated tiefling by the cooper's yard too, though his interest seemed to be in their gate."

He looks over the notice, then back to Hesper.

"I'll leave your seal alone. But I'm not agreeing to rob a moneylender before we've tried speaking to him. How much is owed, and is redemption money separate from our pay?"

He taps Ashby's name on the paper. "Who is he to you or your husband? If we're walking into a quarrel, we need to know whose."

Pell takes the notice, tilts it toward a strip of shutter-light and reads it twice.

"Tiefling, your boy. Road dust on him three days old, watching the cooper's gate as much as your door. He's waiting on someone as well as watching you." He hands the paper on to Bram. "That's what I saw, for what it's worth."

He leans a shoulder on the desk, easy, touching nothing else.

"Now the questions a man asks before he says yes. Thole: does he keep the coffer at the Scales, or does he bank it somewhere with thicker walls? Does he know you by sight? And Ashby. Who is he to your husband that he'd buy a forfeit eight months in the making the very week it falls due? A man doesn't pay for the right to a locked box unless he knows what's in it."

A short pause.

"And the seal. I'll say this plainly so there's no misunderstanding later: I open locks for a living, and I'm telling you I won't open yours. Unopened, seal whole, into your hands. But if Thole's already broken it, or Ashby has, I want to know now what you'd have us do, because I'd rather not learn your answer at sundown with the thing in my arms."

Hesper hears all three of you out without interrupting. Then she takes the questions in the order they were asked, as if ticking down a column.

"The boy at the trough. Yes, that's him. Fourteen or so, bare arms." She glances at Pell. "Not the tiefling, Master Dunmore. I've watched the boy for three days. I only noticed the tiefling yesterday afternoon, and he's never once looked at my windows. I don't know what he's waiting for."

She turns back to Bram.

"How much is owed, I can't tell you. I asked Thole twice. He says the sum is a matter between him and the bearer of the ticket, and I have no ticket. If he'll take money, find out his figure and bring it to me before you pay anything. I won't have a sum paid in my name that I haven't seen. And yes, the redemption is separate. Fifty now and a hundred on delivery is for your work. Anything owed to Thole is my debt to settle."

She lays one finger beside Ashby's name on the notice.

"I don't know him. He's nothing to me, and his name isn't anywhere in Aubrey's papers. People at market say he came to town this spring and buys iron for some firm. That's everything I know. I haven't said he sends the boy, and I won't say it until I know."

She turns to you.

"The seal isn't Thole's, and it isn't Aubrey's notary mark. I know his mark. I sealed his letters with it for twenty years. The wax on the coffer is pale, nearly gold, and there's a sun pressed into it. I never saw him set it, and I don't know whose it is." Her mouth thins. "As for copies, there are none. I've been through his papers twice: his daybook, his letter-book, his drawers. There's no ticket, no receipt, not one line about the Scales. The coffer sat in his study for years. He told me to keep it shut, and I did. One morning last winter he went out with it under his arm and came back without it. He said it was safe. I didn't ask him where. A month later he was dead."

She says that part flatly too, and goes straight on to Pell.

"Thole keeps it at the Scales, in a strongroom behind the counting-room. He showed it to me through a grate, on a shelf. He wanted me to see it was whole, and it was, three days ago. He knows my face. I've been in his shop twice this week, and he was civil both times and gave me nothing." A short pause. "Why a man would buy that forfeit in the very week it falls due, I've asked myself the same question. I don't have an answer for you."

"Your last question is a fair one, so here's the clause. If the seal is broken before the coffer comes into your hands, you bring it to me anyway, and you tell me who broke it. If you can show me it wasn't you, the hundred is still yours. If it breaks in your hands, it isn't."

She takes a small leather purse from the desk drawer and sets it on the blotter. She keeps her hand on it and doesn't push it across.

"Those are the terms. Do you take them?"

Where you are: Hesper Vallow's room, at her desk · Time: Day 1 · morning

Bram speaks first. "I'll take the work on those terms." He glances at you and Pell.

"Give us a short signed note authorising us to speak to Thole for you. He may still refuse, but let's give him one less excuse. And may we carry the notice?"

He settles his shield strap. "I'd start at the Scales. Ask what proof he'll accept without the ticket, find his price, and see whether the seal's still whole. No promises of payment until you've approved the sum."

Pell looks at the purse a moment, then at Hesper's hand on it, and doesn't reach for it yet.

"Gold wax, a sun pressed in it. Your husband died on Lathander's steps." He says it quietly, not as an accusation. "I'd wager the Song of the Morning knows that seal, even if you don't. Worth an hour of someone's day to ask them, before we go kicking on Thole's door."

He straightens off the desk.

"I take the terms. Fifty now, a hundred on delivery, seal whole or the name of who broke it." He glances at Bram and you. "I'd do it in this order, if nobody objects: the Scales first, in daylight, with the door open and honest faces in front. Bram asks Thole his figure, since Thole will take a figure from a man with a shield sooner than from me. While he's naming it, I'd like a look at that grate and the shelf behind it — how the strongroom's built, what the lock is, where the back of the building gives onto. Not to use. To know. If Thole's reasonable, Mistress Vallow pays and that's the end of it. If he isn't, or if Ashby's already been in the room, then we know what we're dealing with before dark instead of after."

When Pell reaches for the purse, Hesper lifts her hand from it and lets him take it. He weighs it once in his palm and tucks it inside his coat.

"Fifty," she says. "Count it if you like."

"One more thing," Pell says. "Your boy at the trough — I'd rather he didn't follow us to the Scales. I'll go out your yard door and come round. Let him count two leaving, not three."

Hesper has heard the three of you out. She sits down at the desk, pulls a clean sheet toward her and dips the pen. She answers the questions in the order they were put to her.

"Master Halloway. Yes, you'll have your note." The pen scratches steadily in a plain clerk's hand, with no flourish on any letter. She doesn't read it back. She turns it round on the blotter so Bram can read it himself:

*To Master Gaspar Thole, at the sign of the Scales. The bearers, Bram Halloway, Sefa Marrin and Pell Dunmore, speak for me in the matter of the iron coffer pledged by my late husband, Aubrey Vallow. They may hear your terms. They may not agree to any sum on my behalf. — Hesper Vallow, widow.*

She signs it and blots it. Her eyes go to the small brass seal-press at the corner of the desk, and she leaves it where it is. "I won't put his mark on it. It isn't mine to use." She folds the note in three and hands it to Bram, with Thole's notice on top. "Carry both. Bring the notice back to me. It's the only paper I have from that man."

She turns to you.

"The boy. He's a child, and I have no quarrel with him. Speak to him if you think it's worth it. Don't do it on my step." That part comes out a little sharper than the rest. "As for seeing the coffer, the grate is Thole's to open, not mine. I've no objection. Whether he'll show it to strangers, I can't say."

She stops. When she answers the last part, she says it as flatly as she spoke of the temple steps.

"You asked yes or no. I can't honestly give you either. He told me to keep it shut, and he never told me why. I've spoken of that coffer to Gaspar Thole, twice, this week. Not to the Fist. Not to the temple. Not to any friend. Now I've spoken of it to you three, and that's everyone."

Last, she turns to Pell.

"The temple. I haven't taken the seal to them. Ask, if you think it's worth an hour. Leave my name out of it if you can." She doesn't explain that. "The yard door is at the end of the passage. It's barred on the inside. It gives onto the yard, and the yard gate onto the back alley that runs behind the lane. You come out near the forges, below the main street, out of sight of the trough."

She caps the inkpot. A strip of light from round the shutter has crept a finger's width across the floor while she wrote.

"The sum comes to me before anything is paid. You know the rest." She folds her ink-stained hands on the blotter. "I'll be here until sundown."

The hall waits for you, with the front door bolted and the yard door barred at the end of the passage. Nothing else happens in the house unless one of you wants it to.

Your journal, new:
+ Goal: Aubrey Vallow's iron coffer
+ Quest: Aubrey Vallow's iron coffer
+ Promise: Return Thole's notice to Hesper

Where you are: Hesper Vallow's house, at her desk · Time: Day 1 · morning

Bram reads the note, then tucks both papers safely away. "You'll have your notice back."

In the hall he speaks quietly to you and Pell. "Sefa, if you want a word with the lad, I'll leave the talking to you. I'll stay a few paces off, close enough to help, not looming over him. Pell, we'll meet you at the Scales unless you've something else in mind."

Pell nods once, like a man who has heard a contract read out and found nothing in it to argue with. "Then I'll see you at sundown, Mistress Vallow. Earlier, if Thole's a reasonable man." A beat. "He won't be. They never are the week the term falls due."

He turns to you and Bram in the dim. "Go out the front, the pair of you, slow and plain, the way you came. Let the boy have his count. Sefa, if you want your two minutes with him, take them on the walk, away from this step, as the lady asks. I'll be at the Scales before you are. Don't look for me; I'll find you. If I'm not at Thole's counter when you get there, I'm looking at the back of his building, and I'll come in the front door like a customer when I'm done."

To Hesper, already moving toward the passage: "The Scales: which street, and what's it stand between? I'd rather not ask a cooper for directions with a tiefling leaning on his wall."

Hesper answers you first. "I'll tell anyone who asks that I've hired help. Your names are nobody's business, and they won't get them from me." Then, to Pell, as he's already turning for the passage: "Main street, toward the temple. Four doors past the Red Sheaf, on the same side, between a chandler's and a saddler's. A brass scale hangs over the door." She doesn't answer what he said about Thole being unreasonable.

Pell doesn't wait for the bolt. He's gone down the passage before Bram reaches the front door.

Bram slides the bolt and opens the door onto full morning. After the dim hall the lane is very bright. Hammers ring and the smoke comes up from the forges. He looks up the lane, leaving his sword sheathed.

The boy is still on the trough rim, bare arms and all. So is the tiefling, his back to the cooper's wall and his tail wound round his boot.

You step out first and Bram follows, a couple of paces behind and off to the side. The shield hangs low on his arm. Behind you the door shuts, and you hear the bolt go home.

You're halfway up the lane when the tiefling notices you. A woman, and a big man in chain, coming straight up the lane toward his corner. He straightens off the wall and takes half a step toward the cooper's gate, as if he means to knock at last. Then he stops and stays where he is, looking anywhere but at Bram. He has the stiff face of a man who has been moved on from corners before.

The boy took in the door opening. Now he slides off the trough rim, cups water in both hands and splashes it over his forearms. He scrubs at them as if nothing in Beregost matters more than this. He keeps his head down. His feet are under him, though, and his weight is on the side toward the main street.

You reach the top of the lane. The trough is a few steps away, and the boy is close enough to hear you without anyone raising their voice. He hasn't run yet.

Where you are: top of the lane, by the trough · Time: Day 1 · morning

Behind you, Bram stops a few paces short of the trough, where you want him, leaving the boy's way onto the main street clear. He turns slightly aside, shield held low, and says nothing. His eyes move to the street beyond the boy.

You stop a stride short of the trough with one hand raised a little behind you. The boy keeps scrubbing his forearms, slower now, and listens without looking up. His eyes come up at "I'm not Watch." He looks at you, then over your shoulder at Bram's shield, then back at your hands.

[Out of game] Thanks, that's a vivid picture of the boy, and I can see the scene you're hoping for. I can't take it as what happens, though. What he says, what he knows and whether he stays are mine to play, and the die on your card decides how he takes Sefa's approach. The card is still waiting, and I'm keeping it: a nervous lad with his weight already on the main-street side might well bolt from a stranger, so the outcome is genuinely uncertain.

What I need from you is Sefa's side of the moment. What does she say to him as she reaches the trough, and how does she stand? Does the copper come out at once, or only after he's spoken? Write that as Sefa, then press the roll. I'll play the boy from that and from the result, in the next turn.

One thing I'll say now so it doesn't surprise you later: anything he knows comes from what he could actually have seen or been told. He doesn't simply know what happened inside the house or by the back way. Whatever he reveals, I'll make sure it has a source.

The boy takes his weight off the street-side foot. Not much, but he does it.

"He's not my friend." He jerks his chin at the tiefling without turning his head. "Don't know him. He's been stood there since yesterday looking at Dobb's gate like it owes him money." He wipes his wet hands down his shirt and looks you over again, the beads, the plain knife, your face. "I'm Wat."

He glances once along the main street toward the Red Sheaf, then back.

"A copper's a copper," he says, and his ears go a little red. "But I get a silver for sitting here. I'm not giving that up for one copper and a talk." He keeps his voice under the hammers, the way you did. "And I'm not walking off anywhere with him." He means Bram. "You want to talk, we talk here, by the trough, where people can see. And you don't tell anyone I did. Nobody. Swear it?"

He stays put, rubbing the water off his arms. He's waiting for your answer, and his feet are still ready to run, but he doesn't bolt for the main street.

Behind you, Bram keeps his eyes past the boy, on the main street.

Where you are: a stride from the trough, talking with Wat · Time: Day 1 · morning

The big man gives Wat a small nod. "You needn't go anywhere with me." It gets a wary flick of the eyes from Wat and nothing else. Bram walks back a few paces toward the lane, keeping you in sight and looking down the main street, and as he goes the boy's shoulders come down a little.

At the trough, Wat looks at the silver between your fingers. Then he looks at your face. The tips of his ears go red.
